# LoadPR: full text (English)

> Load your barbell right, instantly

LoadPR is an iPhone app that works out which plates to load on a barbell and tracks your personal records (PRs). This site adds free browser calculators for loading a barbell in kilograms or pounds: a plate calculator, a home gym plate calculator for the plates you own, a one-rep max (1RM) calculator, a 1RM percentage calculator, a 5/3/1 calculator, a warmup calculator, a kg to lb converter and a "what's on the bar" calculator that adds up a loaded barbell. The app is free to download, with optional in-app purchases. Contact: support@loadpr.com.

Every page below is on loadpr.com at the URL given. All weights and percentages come from the same engine as the calculators, so the numbers match the site and the app.

# Tools

## Barbell plate calculator

URL: https://loadpr.com/plate-calculator/

Enter a target weight and we'll show exactly which plates go on each side. If it isn't loadable with your plates, we show the closest weight you can hit.

### How much does the bar weigh?

A standard men's Olympic bar weighs **20 kg** (45 lb) and the women's bar **15 kg** (33 lb). Technique and training bars weigh 10 to 15 kg. Always add the bar to the total: 100 kg on the bar is 40 kg of plates per side plus the 20 kg bar.

### Plates per side, not in total

A barbell is loaded symmetrically: every plate you put on one side goes on the other too. That's why this calculator gives you plates **per side**. For 60 kg with a 20 kg bar you need 20 kg per side: one 20 kg plate on each end.

### Olympic plate colors

Under the IWF standard, competition plates follow a color code: **25 kg red, 20 kg blue, 15 kg yellow, 10 kg green**. Our diagram uses the same colors so you can read a load at a glance.

---

## One-rep max (1RM) calculator

URL: https://loadpr.com/1rm-calculator/

Enter weight and reps to estimate your one-rep max and see your training percentages.

### Which formula should you use?

There is no perfect formula. **Epley** and **Brzycki** are the most widely used and agree closely at low reps. Above 8–10 reps every estimate loses accuracy: treat it as a reference, not a hard truth.

---

## Warmup set calculator

URL: https://loadpr.com/warmup-calculator/

Enter your working weight and we'll build your warmup sets, rounded to the nearest loadable plate.

### Why warm up progressively

Raising the weight step by step primes your nervous system and joints without building fatigue. A good warmup doesn't tire you out: it leaves you ready for your working set.

---

## Kg to lb converter

URL: https://loadpr.com/kg-to-lb/

Convert between kilograms and pounds instantly. Perfect for reading a program written in the other unit.

### The exact equivalence

1 kg = 2.2046 lb and 1 lb = 0.4536 kg. A 20 kg plate is 44.09 lb, not 45 lb, which is why a bar loaded in kilos never matches one loaded in pounds exactly.

---

## 1RM percentage calculator

URL: https://loadpr.com/1rm-percentage-calculator/

Enter your one-rep max to see every training percentage, plus the nearest weight you can actually load with standard plates.

### Why round to a loadable weight

Percentages rarely land on a weight you can load. 95% of a 140 kg max is 133 kg, but with 1.25 kg as the smallest plate the bar moves in 2.5 kg steps, so the closest load is **132.5 kg**. In pounds the step is 5 lb with 2.5 lb plates.

### Choosing a range

Programs written in percentages often put heavy sets above 80% of your max and volume or technique work below it. Pick the range and step that match your program: 5% for a quick overview, 2.5% for finer steps.

---

## What's on the bar? Loaded barbell calculator

URL: https://loadpr.com/whats-on-the-bar/

Walked up to a loaded bar? Add the plates you see on one side and get the total, with the bar and collars counted in.

### Count one side, double it

A barbell is loaded the same on both ends, so you only need to count one side. The total is the bar, plus both collars, plus twice the plates on one side: 20 kg + 2 × (20 + 10) = **80 kg**.

### Kilo plates in a pound gym

A 20 kg plate is 44.09 lb, so a bar loaded in kilos almost never reads as a round number in pounds. The total is shown in both units so you can compare it with your program.

---

## Home gym plate calculator

URL: https://loadpr.com/home-gym-plate-calculator/

Tell us how many plates of each size you own. We find the exact load with the fewest plates, even when starting with the heaviest plate doesn't work.

### Why heaviest-first can fail

With two 25 kg and four 15 kg plates, 80 kg on a 20 kg bar needs 30 kg per side. Starting with a 25 leaves 5 kg you don't have, but **15 + 15** per side works. This calculator checks every combination your plates allow.

### Count plates, not pairs

Enter the total number of plates you own of each size. Each side needs its own plate, so three 10 kg plates still give you one pair.

---

## 5/3/1 calculator

URL: https://loadpr.com/531-calculator/

Enter your one-rep max. We take the training max, lay out the three weeks and the deload, and show the plates for every set, rounded to weights you can load.

### Why the weights look lower than your max

5/3/1 takes every percentage from the **training max**, 90% of your 1RM, not from the 1RM itself. A 455 lb deadlift gives a 409.5 lb training max, so week 1's top set at 85% is 348.08 lb, loaded as **350 lb**. The [5/3/1 training max guide](https://loadpr.com/guide/531-training-max/) explains 90% versus 85%.

### After each cycle

Add 5 lb (2.5 kg) to the training max for the bench press and overhead press, and 10 lb (5 kg) for the squat and deadlift, then run the next cycle. The calculator shows the next training max for the lift you pick.

### Supplemental work

First Set Last repeats the first working set of the week for 5 sets of 5. Boring But Big adds 5 sets of 10 at 50% of the training max. Neither runs in the deload week.

# Guides

## Olympic plate colors: the complete guide

URL: https://loadpr.com/guide/olympic-plate-colors/

Updated 2026-10-28

Competition plates follow the color code of the International Weightlifting Federation (IWF). Knowing the colors lets you read the load on a bar without walking over to check the numbers.

### Main plates

- **25 kg — red** (55 lb)
- **20 kg — blue** (44 lb)
- **15 kg — yellow** (33 lb)
- **10 kg — green** (22 lb)
- **5 kg — white** (11 lb)

### Change plates

The small plates (2.5 / 2 / 1.5 / 1 / 0.5 kg) repeat the same color sequence at a smaller size and are used to adjust the load in fine increments during competition. In a regular gym your smallest plate sets the smallest jump, which is [why you can't load an exact weight on a barbell](https://loadpr.com/guide/cant-load-exact-weight/) without change plates.

### What about regular gyms?

Outside competition, most plates are black rubber bumpers or bare iron with no color. The IWF code is only mandatory at sanctioned meets, though many pound-denominated bumper sets borrow it: 45 lb blue, 35 lb yellow, 25 lb green, 10 lb white. Whatever its color, a plate weighs what is stamped on it: [how much a plate weighs](https://loadpr.com/guide/how-much-does-a-plate-weigh/) lists every plate in kg and lb.

### Sources

- [IPF Technical Rulebook (2026)](https://www.powerlifting.sport/fileadmin/ipf/data/rules/technical-rules/english/2026_IPF_Technical_Rulebook__effective_01_March_2026__v3.pdf)
- [Olympic weightlifting: equipment (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_weightlifting)

### FAQ

**What color is the 20 kg plate?**
Blue. It's the standard Olympic plate for most working loads.

**How much does the red plate weigh?**
25 kg (55 lb) under the IWF color code for main plates.

---

## How much does a barbell weigh?

URL: https://loadpr.com/guide/barbell-weights/

Updated 2026-10-25

**Short answer: a standard Olympic barbell weighs 45 lb (20 kg).** That's the long bar in almost every gym's squat rack, bench press and deadlift platform. The women's Olympic bar weighs 33 lb (15 kg). Every other bar is in the table below.

### Barbell weights at a glance

| Bar | lb | kg |
|---|---|---|
| Men's Olympic bar (7.2 ft / 2.2 m) | 45 | 20 |
| Women's Olympic bar (6.6 ft / 2.01 m) | 33 | 15 |
| Technique / training bar | 15–33 | 7–15 |
| EZ curl bar | 15–25 | 7–11 |
| Hex (trap) bar | 45–60 | 20–27 |
| Safety squat bar | 55–70 | 25–32 |
| Standard 1-inch bar (home sets) | 15–25 | 7–11 |
| Smith machine bar | varies, often 15–25 | varies, often 7–11 |

### Is the bar at the gym 45 lb?

Almost always, yes. The long bar with rotating sleeves in the squat rack and on the bench is a men's Olympic bar: 45 lb (20 kg). Shorter, thinner bars without rotating sleeves (about 1 inch thick) are lighter, usually 15–25 lb. If a bar has no stamp, check the end cap or ask the staff.

### Bench press and squat bars

Both use the same 45 lb (20 kg) Olympic bar unless your gym has a specialty bar, and the bar counts toward your total: an empty bar on the bench is already 45 lb. Some dedicated powerlifting squat bars are thicker and weigh 55 lb (25 kg); deadlift bars are usually 45 lb (20 kg).

### The bar counts in every total

The bar is part of the load. With a 45 lb bar and 45 lb plates (or a 20 kg bar and 20 kg plates):

| Plates per side | lb | kg |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 135 | 60 |
| 2 | 225 | 100 |

For 3 to 6 plates, kilo totals and 25 lb plates, see [how much is 1 to 6 plates on each side](https://loadpr.com/guide/plates-on-each-side/). For any other load, the [plate calculator](https://loadpr.com/plate-calculator/) counts the bar for you. Training in the other unit? Use the [kg ↔ lb converter](https://loadpr.com/kg-to-lb/).

If you don't know your bar's exact weight, pick "Custom" in the calculator and enter it by hand. Collars add to the total too: see [how much barbell collars weigh](https://loadpr.com/guide/barbell-collar-weight/).

### Sources

- [IPF Technical Rulebook (2026)](https://www.powerlifting.sport/fileadmin/ipf/data/rules/technical-rules/english/2026_IPF_Technical_Rulebook__effective_01_March_2026__v3.pdf)
- [Barbell (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbell)

### FAQ

**How much does a standard barbell weigh?**
A standard men's Olympic barbell weighs 45 lb (20 kg). The women's Olympic bar weighs 33 lb (15 kg).

**Does the bar count toward the total weight?**
Yes. A 45 lb bar with one 45 lb plate on each side is 135 lb in total.

**How much does an EZ curl bar weigh?**
About 15–25 lb (7–11 kg), depending on the model.

**How much does a trap bar weigh?**
A hex (trap) bar usually weighs 45–60 lb (20–27 kg).

**How much does a Smith machine bar weigh?**
It depends on the machine. Many are around 15–25 lb, and counterbalanced ones can be lighter. Check the label on the machine.

---

## Kg ↔ lb equivalents for the gym

URL: https://loadpr.com/guide/kg-to-lb-equivalents/

Updated 2026-10-28

Plenty of programs are written in the other unit. This guide helps you translate loads without losing precision.

### The conversion

1 kg = 2.2046 lb. To go from kilos to pounds multiply by 2.2046; for the other direction multiply by 0.4536.

### Common loads

- 60 kg ≈ 132 lb
- 100 kg ≈ 220 lb
- 140 kg ≈ 309 lb
- 135 lb ≈ 61 kg
- 225 lb ≈ 102 kg
- 315 lb ≈ 143 kg

Remember: kg plates and lb plates don't line up, so a loaded bar is rarely a round number in both units. Use the converter for the exact value, then round to the [nearest loadable weight](https://loadpr.com/guide/cant-load-exact-weight/) for your plates.

### Sources

- [Pound (mass): 1 lb = 0.45359237 kg (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pound_(mass))

### FAQ

**How many pounds is 100 kg?**
About 220.5 lb.

**How many kilos is 225 lb?**
About 102 kg.

---

## How much is 1 to 6 plates on each side?

URL: https://loadpr.com/guide/plates-on-each-side/

Updated 2026-10-25

**Short answer: with a 45 lb bar and 45 lb plates, 1 plate on each side is 135 lb, 2 plates are 225 lb, 3 plates are 315 lb, 4 plates are 405 lb, 5 plates are 495 lb and 6 plates are 585 lb.** In the gym, "a plate" means one 45 lb plate (a 20 kg plate in a kilo gym), and lifters count the plates on one side of the bar. In kilos, 2 plates on each side of a 20 kg bar is 100 kg.

### How to work it out: 3 plates on each side

Add the plates on one side, double that for both sides, then add the bar:

- Plates on one side: 45 + 45 + 45 = 135 lb.
- Both sides: 2 × 135 = 270 lb.
- Add the bar: 270 + 45 = **315 lb**.

The same steps work for any count: 1 plate is 45 + 2 × 45 = 135 lb, and 2 plates are 45 + 2 × 90 = 225 lb. Every extra 45 lb plate on each side adds 90 lb to the bar, because it goes on both ends.

### Plates on each side in pounds

A 45 lb Olympic bar with 45 lb plates. Each total links to the plate breakdown for that weight:

| Plates per side | Total (lb) | Plates on the bar |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 135 | 2 |
| 2 | 225 | 4 |
| 3 | 315 | 6 |
| 4 | 405 | 8 |
| 5 | 495 | 10 |
| 6 | 585 | 12 |

405 lb is the "four plates" milestone and 495 lb is five plates. How many plates fit on one sleeve depends on the bar and on how thick the plates are.

### Plates on each side in kg

In a kilo gym "a plate" is usually the 20 kg plate on a 20 kg bar. If you are asking how much N plates is in kg with pound plates, the last column converts the pound totals above:

| Plates per side | 20 kg plates, 20 kg bar | 45 lb plates, 45 lb bar, in kg |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 60 kg | 61.24 kg |
| 2 | 100 kg | 102.06 kg |
| 3 | 140 kg | 142.88 kg |
| 4 | 180 kg | 183.7 kg |
| 5 | 220 kg | 224.53 kg |
| 6 | 260 kg | 265.35 kg |

So 5 plates in kg is 220 kg with 20 kg plates, or 224.53 kg if the plates are 45 lb ones. A 20 kg plate weighs 44.09 lb, a little less than a 45 lb plate (see [how much a plate weighs](https://loadpr.com/guide/how-much-does-a-plate-weigh/)). Some kilo gyms load 25 kg plates instead: one 25 kg plate on each side of a 20 kg bar is 70 kg, and two are 120 kg.

### With 25 lb plates

Lighter plates add up the same way. On a 45 lb bar:

| 25 lb plates per side | Total (lb) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 95 |
| 2 | 145 |
| 3 | 195 |
| 4 | 245 |

Mixed plates work too: one 45 and one 25 on each side is 185 lb, and two 45s and a 25 on each side is 275 lb. For any mix, [what's on the bar](https://loadpr.com/whats-on-the-bar/) adds it up for you, and the [plate calculator](https://loadpr.com/plate-calculator/) goes the other way, from a target weight to the plates per side.

### Bench press: how much is 2 plates?

Bench, squat and deadlift use the same 45 lb bar in most gyms, so the numbers do not change: a 2 plate bench is 225 lb and a 3 plate squat is 315 lb. A 1 plate bench is 135 lb. If your bench bar weighs something else, use its weight instead of 45 lb; [how much a barbell weighs](https://loadpr.com/guide/barbell-weights/) lists the common bars.

### Common mistakes

- **Mixing up plates per side and plates in total.** "4 plates" usually means four on each side (405 lb). If someone means four plates in total, two on each side, that is 225 lb. Ask which one they mean.
- **Forgetting the bar.** Two 45s on each side are 180 lb of plates; the bar makes it 225 lb.
- **Assuming every bar weighs 45 lb.** A women's Olympic bar is 33 lb (15 kg), so 2 plates on each side of it are 213 lb. In kilos, 2 × 20 kg on each side of a 15 kg bar is 95 kg.
- **Leaving out collars.** Collars add a little weight, and how much depends on the model. Count them when you need an exact total.
- **Mixing kg and lb plates.** A 20 kg plate is not a 45 lb plate. Convert with the [kg to lb converter](https://loadpr.com/kg-to-lb/) before you add them up.

### Loading it with the LoadPR app

The tables on this page are plain arithmetic, with as many 45s as the load needs. The LoadPR app's free plate set has two of each plate per side (45, 35, 25, 10, 5 and 2.5 lb, or 25 down to 1.25 kg), so a load like 225 lb comes straight from it. With LoadPR+ you can enter the plates your gym actually has.

### FAQ

**How much is 2 plates on each side?**
225 lb with a 45 lb bar and two 45 lb plates on each side. In kilos, two 20 kg plates on each side of a 20 kg bar make 100 kg.

**How much is 1 plate on each side?**
135 lb: a 45 lb bar plus one 45 lb plate on each side. With a 20 kg bar and 20 kg plates it is 60 kg.

**How much weight is 4 plates?**
405 lb when it means four 45 lb plates on each side of a 45 lb bar. If it means four plates in total, two on each side, it is 225 lb.

**How much is 5 plates in kg?**
220 kg with five 20 kg plates on each side of a 20 kg bar. Five 45 lb plates on each side of a 45 lb bar make 495 lb, which is 224.53 kg.

**How much is 6 plates on each side?**
585 lb with six 45 lb plates on each side of a 45 lb bar, or 260 kg with six 20 kg plates on each side of a 20 kg bar.

---

## How much does a weight plate weigh?

URL: https://loadpr.com/guide/how-much-does-a-plate-weigh/

Updated 2026-10-25

**Short answer: the big plate in most gyms weighs 45 lb, which is 20.41 kg. In a kilo gym the matching plate is 20 kg, which is 44.09 lb.** When lifters say "a plate" they mean one of these. A plate weighs what is stamped on it, and the tables below give every common plate in both units.

### Why a 45 lb plate is not 20 kg

Pound plates are made in round pounds and kilo plates in round kilos, so the two big plates are close but not equal. One kilogram is 2.2046 lb:

- 45 lb ÷ 2.2046 = **20.41 kg**
- 20 kg × 2.2046 = **44.09 lb**

The gap is small for one plate and grows as you load more. A 45 lb bar with two 45s on each side is 225 lb, which is 102.06 kg. A 20 kg bar with two 20 kg plates on each side is 100 kg, which is 220.46 lb. Both get called "two plates", but they are not the same load.

### Pound plates in kg

| Plate | Weight in kg |
|---|---|
| 45 lb | 20.41 |
| 35 lb | 15.88 |
| 25 lb | 11.34 |
| 10 lb | 4.54 |
| 5 lb | 2.27 |
| 2.5 lb | 1.13 |

A 25 lb plate is 11.34 kg and a 10 lb plate is 4.54 kg, so pound plates never land on round kilos.

### Kilo plates in pounds

| Plate | Weight in lb |
|---|---|
| 25 kg | 55.12 |
| 20 kg | 44.09 |
| 15 kg | 33.07 |
| 10 kg | 22.05 |
| 5 kg | 11.02 |
| 2.5 kg | 5.51 |
| 1.25 kg | 2.76 |

The 25 kg plate (55.12 lb) is heavier than a 45 lb plate, which surprises lifters who move from a pound gym to a kilo gym. On competition plates the colors tell them apart: 25 kg is red and 20 kg is blue (see [Olympic plate colors](https://loadpr.com/guide/olympic-plate-colors/)).

### A plate's weight vs the bar total

The number on a plate is the weight of that one plate, not the weight on the bar. The load you lift is the bar plus every plate on both ends, so a pair of 45 lb plates adds 90 lb to the bar, and a pair of 20 kg plates adds 40 kg. For bar totals with 1 to 6 plates on each side, see [how much is 1 to 6 plates on each side](https://loadpr.com/guide/plates-on-each-side/).

### Bumper plates vs iron plates

A 45 lb bumper and a 45 lb iron plate weigh the same. The bumper is made of rubber, which is lighter for its size than iron, so it is thicker and takes more room on the sleeve; how thick depends on the model. Most full-size bumpers are 450 mm (about 17.7 in) across, the competition size, so the bar sits at the same height whichever bumper is on it; some light bumpers are smaller. Competition (calibrated) plates are made to a tight weight tolerance. Ordinary gym plates can be off by a little, and how much depends on the maker.

### Olympic and standard plates

A 45 lb plate with a 2-inch hole (Olympic) and a 45 lb plate with a 1-inch hole (standard) weigh the same. The hole decides which bar the plate fits, not what it weighs. See [Olympic vs standard plates](https://loadpr.com/guide/olympic-vs-standard-plates/).

### Common mistakes

- **Treating 20 kg and 45 lb as equal.** A 20 kg plate is 44.09 lb, not 45, and on a heavy bar the difference adds up.
- **Rounding a kilo to 2 lb.** A kilo is 2.2046 lb, so a 20 kg plate is 44.09 lb, not 40.
- **Leaving out the bar.** The plates are only part of the load; a 45 lb bar with one 45 on each side is 135 lb.
- **Reading the wrong number.** Some plates are stamped in both lb and kg. Check which unit is the main one before you add them up, or use the [kg to lb converter](https://loadpr.com/kg-to-lb/).

### Sources

- [Pound (mass): 1 lb = 0.45359237 kg (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pound_(mass))

### FAQ

**How much does a 45 lb plate weigh in kg?**
20.41 kg. One kilogram is 2.2046 lb, so 45 lb divided by 2.2046 is 20.41 kg.

**How much does a 20 kg plate weigh in pounds?**
44.09 lb, slightly less than a 45 lb plate.

**How many kg is 1 plate?**
One 45 lb plate is 20.41 kg. In a kilo gym, one plate usually means a 20 kg plate, which is 44.09 lb.

**How much does a 25 kg plate weigh in pounds?**
55.12 lb, so it is heavier than a 45 lb plate (20.41 kg).

**Do bumper plates weigh the same as iron plates?**
Yes. A 45 lb bumper weighs 45 lb (20.41 kg), the same as a 45 lb iron plate. The bumper is thicker because rubber is lighter for its size than iron.

---

## Olympic vs standard plates: what is the difference?

URL: https://loadpr.com/guide/olympic-vs-standard-plates/

Updated 2026-10-25

**Short answer: the difference is the hole. Olympic plates have a 2-inch (50 mm) center hole and fit Olympic bars, like the 45 lb (20 kg) bar in a commercial gym. Standard plates have a 1-inch hole and fit standard bars, the thinner 15–25 lb bars in many home sets.** A 45 lb Olympic plate and a 45 lb standard plate weigh the same; they just do not fit the same bar.

### Example: the same plates on each bar

Put one 25 lb and one 10 lb plate on each side. The plates weigh the same on both bars, so only the bar changes the total:

- Olympic bar, 45 lb: 45 + 2 × (25 + 10) = **115 lb**
- Standard bar, 20 lb (check yours, they vary): 20 + 2 × (25 + 10) = **90 lb**

Most of the difference between two setups is the bar. [How much a barbell weighs](https://loadpr.com/guide/barbell-weights/) lists the common bars, and the [home gym plate calculator](https://loadpr.com/home-gym-plate-calculator/) works out a load from the plates you own.

### Olympic vs standard at a glance

|  | Olympic | Standard |
|---|---|---|
| Center hole | About 2 in (50 mm) | About 1 in |
| Bar | Olympic bar: 45 lb (20 kg) men's, 33 lb (15 kg) women's | Standard bar: usually 15–25 lb (7–11 kg) |
| Sleeves | Thick sleeves that rotate | About as thick as the bar, usually fixed |
| Where you see them | Commercial gyms, weightlifting and powerlifting | Many beginner and home sets |

### Can you put Olympic plates on a standard bar?

Not safely. A 2-inch hole on a 1-inch bar leaves the plate loose, so it slides and rattles, and standard collars are not made to hold it. Standard plates do not fit an Olympic bar at all: a 1-inch hole will not go over a 2-inch sleeve. Some makers sell adapter sleeves for a standard bar; they add their own weight, and the bar's rated load still applies.

### Which one to buy for a home gym

Olympic plates fit the bars in commercial gyms, so your numbers carry over, and there are more bars, racks and bumper plates made for them. Standard sets are lighter, take less room and often cost less to start with, but a standard bar is usually rated for less weight than an Olympic bar; the exact rating depends on the model. If you plan to lift heavy, Olympic is the usual choice.

### Olympic plates in kg and lb

Olympic plates come in both units. Pound sets usually run 45, 35, 25, 10, 5 and 2.5 lb; kilo sets 25, 20, 15, 10, 5, 2.5 and 1.25 kg. A 45 lb plate is 20.41 kg and a 20 kg plate is 44.09 lb, so the two are close but not the same; [how much a plate weighs](https://loadpr.com/guide/how-much-does-a-plate-weigh/) lists every plate in both units. On competition plates the color shows the weight ([Olympic plate colors](https://loadpr.com/guide/olympic-plate-colors/)).

### Common mistakes

- **Thinking "Olympic" means competition plates.** In most gyms it only means the 2-inch hole. Competition plates are a stricter kind of Olympic plate, with set sizes and colors.
- **Assuming every bar weighs 45 lb.** A standard bar is usually 15–25 lb, so the same plates make a lighter total.
- **Buying plates before the bar.** Check the bar's sleeves first; the plates have to match them.
- **Mixing units.** Kilo and pound Olympic plates both fit an Olympic bar, so a mixed bar is easy to load by mistake. Convert with the [kg to lb converter](https://loadpr.com/kg-to-lb/).

### Bars and plates in the LoadPR app

The free setup in the LoadPR app is a 45 lb (or 20 kg) Olympic bar with two of each plate per side. If you train with a standard bar or your own plate set, LoadPR+ lets you add custom bars and plates (see [gyms and plates](https://loadpr.com/features/gyms-and-plates/)).

### Sources

- [Barbell (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbell)

### FAQ

**What is the difference between Olympic and standard plates?**
The center hole. Olympic plates have a 2-inch (50 mm) hole for Olympic bars; standard plates have a 1-inch hole for standard bars. A 45 lb plate weighs 45 lb either way.

**Do Olympic plates fit a standard bar?**
No. A 2-inch hole is loose on a 1-inch bar and the plate will slide. Use plates that match the bar, or a standard set on a standard bar.

**Can I use standard plates on an Olympic bar?**
No. A 1-inch hole does not fit over the 2-inch sleeve of an Olympic bar, so a 45 lb (20 kg) Olympic bar needs Olympic plates.

**Is a 45 lb Olympic plate heavier than a 45 lb standard plate?**
No. Both weigh 45 lb (20.41 kg). Only the hole size, and often the shape, differ.

**Why are Olympic plates called Olympic?**
They fit the 2-inch bar used in Olympic weightlifting. In most gyms the name just means the 2-inch hole; competition plates add strict sizes and colors on top of that.

---

## How much do barbell collars weigh?

URL: https://loadpr.com/guide/barbell-collar-weight/

Updated 2026-10-25

**Short answer: a competition collar weighs 2.5 kg (5.51 lb), so a pair adds 5 kg (11.02 lb) to the bar.** That is the collar used in weightlifting and powerlifting meets, where it counts toward the weight on the bar. The spring clips and lock-jaw collars in most gyms are much lighter, and their exact weight depends on the model.

### Example: one plate on each side with competition collars

Take a 20 kg bar, one 20 kg plate on each side and a 2.5 kg competition collar on each end. Count the bar, both collars and both plates:

- 20 + 2 × 2.5 + 2 × 20 = **65 kg**
- Without the collars it is 20 + 2 × 20 = 60 kg.

The same works backwards. To load 100 kg with competition collars, take the bar and both collars off first: 100 − 20 − 2 × 2.5 = 75 kg of plates, or 37.5 kg on each side. That is **25 + 10 + 2.5 kg per side**. Without collars, 100 kg is 40 kg per side: 25 + 15 kg.

### Collar weights by type

| Collar | Weight |
|---|---|
| Competition collar | 2.5 kg each (5.51 lb), 5 kg a pair (11.02 lb) |
| Spring clip | Depends on the model; far lighter than a competition collar |
| Lock-jaw or clamp collar | Depends on the model |
| Screw-on collar for a 1-inch bar | Depends on the model |

Competition collars are used on competition bars at weightlifting and powerlifting meets. Spring clips are the ones in most commercial gyms, lock-jaw and clamp collars turn up in gyms and home gyms, and screw-on collars come with home sets built on standard 1-inch bars.

If you need an exact total with clips or clamps, weigh a pair on a kitchen or luggage scale, or check the maker’s listing.

### Do collars count toward the weight on the bar?

In competition they do. At IWF weightlifting and IPF powerlifting meets the bar is 20 kg and each collar is 2.5 kg, so an empty bar with collars is already 25 kg. Every attempt includes them:

| Plates on each side | Without collars | With 2.5 kg collars |
|---|---|---|
| None | 20 kg | 25 kg |
| 1 × 20 kg | 60 kg | 65 kg |
| 1 × 25 kg | 70 kg | 75 kg |
| 2 × 25 kg | 120 kg | 125 kg |
| 3 × 25 kg | 170 kg | 175 kg |

In training it is your choice. Light spring clips change the total so little that most lifters leave them out. What matters is doing the same thing every time, so that a number in your log means the same load next month.

### Collars in a pound gym

Competition collars are made in kilos, so in a pound gym they add 11.02 lb for the pair. A 45 lb bar with two 45 lb plates on each side is 225 lb; with competition collars it is 236.02 lb. If you train in pounds but compete in kilos, count the collars when you work out your openers. The [kg to lb converter](https://loadpr.com/kg-to-lb/) handles the rest of the conversion, and [how much a plate weighs](https://loadpr.com/guide/how-much-does-a-plate-weigh/) lists every plate in both units.

### How to enter collars in the plate calculator

The [plate calculator](https://loadpr.com/plate-calculator/) has a field called **Collars (per side)**. Enter the weight of one collar, in the unit the calculator is set to: 2.5 for competition collars in kilos, or 0 to leave them out. The calculator counts a collar on each end, takes both off the target and then splits the rest into plates. With a 20 kg bar, 100 kg and 2.5 in the field, it shows 25 + 10 + 2.5 kg per side, as in the example above.

The same field is on [what’s on the bar](https://loadpr.com/whats-on-the-bar/), which adds up a loaded bar, and on the [home gym plate calculator](https://loadpr.com/home-gym-plate-calculator/). Switching between kg and lb resets the field to 0, so enter it again in the new unit.

### Why use collars at all?

Collars stop the plates from sliding along the sleeve. A plate that creeps outward on one side makes the bar uneven, and on a fast lift or a missed rep plates can slide off. That is why meets require them, and why many gyms ask you to use them on squats, presses and Olympic lifts. The bar’s own weight is covered in [how much a barbell weighs](https://loadpr.com/guide/barbell-weights/).

### Common mistakes

- **Counting one collar.** There is a collar on each end, so a pair of 2.5 kg collars adds 5 kg, not 2.5 kg.
- **Entering the pair in a per-side field.** The calculator field takes one collar. Typing 5 for competition collars counts 10 kg.
- **Assuming every collar weighs 2.5 kg.** Only competition collars do. Gym clips weigh far less, and clamps depend on the model.
- **Mixing units.** A 2.5 kg collar is 5.51 lb, not 5 lb. Enter it in the unit your calculator uses.
- **Changing how you count.** If you counted collars last month and leave them out today, your numbers stop being comparable.

### Sources

- [IPF Technical Rulebook (2026)](https://www.powerlifting.sport/fileadmin/ipf/data/rules/technical-rules/english/2026_IPF_Technical_Rulebook__effective_01_March_2026__v3.pdf)

### FAQ

**How much does a competition collar weigh?**
A competition collar weighs 2.5 kg (5.51 lb). A pair adds 5 kg (11.02 lb) to the bar.

**Do collars count in a powerlifting meet?**
Yes. At IPF meets the 20 kg bar and two 2.5 kg collars make 25 kg before any plates go on, so one 20 kg plate on each side is 65 kg.

**How much do spring clips weigh?**
It depends on the model, and they are far lighter than a 2.5 kg competition collar. For an exact total, weigh a pair on a scale.

**How many plates per side for 100 kg with competition collars?**
25 + 10 + 2.5 kg on each side of a 20 kg bar. The collars take 5 kg, leaving 37.5 kg per side.

**What goes in the collars field of a plate calculator?**
The weight of one collar, such as 2.5 for competition collars in kg. The calculator counts one on each end, so 2.5 adds 5 kg in total.

---

## What is a 1RM (one-rep max)?

URL: https://loadpr.com/guide/what-is-1rm/

Updated 2026-10-25

**Short answer: 1RM means one-repetition maximum, the heaviest weight you can lift for one full rep with good form.** It is sometimes typed 1 RPM or 1 rm, but it is the same thing. Strength programs use it as a reference point: a workout of 5 sets at 80% means 80% of your 1RM for that lift.

### Example: estimating a 1RM from a set of 5

You do not have to lift your max to know roughly what it is. Say you bench 100 kg for 5 reps. The Epley formula estimates a 1RM from a set like this:

- 1RM = weight × (1 + reps ÷ 30)
- 100 × (1 + 5 ÷ 30) = **116.67 kg**

So a lifter who can bench 100 kg for 5 could probably bench about 116.67 kg once. It is an estimate, not a promise. For your own numbers and other formulas, use the [1RM calculator](https://loadpr.com/1rm-calculator/).

### Tested vs estimated 1RM

There are two ways to get the number, and they answer slightly different questions.

|  | Tested 1RM | Estimated 1RM |
|---|---|---|
| How you get it | Work up to one heavy single | Put a set of a few reps into a formula |
| How exact it is | Exact for that day | Close at low reps, rougher above 8 to 10 reps |
| How tiring it is | Very: it needs warm-ups and recovery | Normal: it comes from a set you do anyway |
| Typical use | Meets, testing weeks | Setting training loads between tests |

A tested max is real, but it costs a session and needs a spotter or safety arms. An estimate is free, but different formulas give different answers, and none of them is reliable for sets of 15 or 20.

### 1RM vs a rep PR

A 1RM is a single. A rep PR is the most you have lifted for some other number of reps, such as your best set of 5. Both are personal records, and a rep PR can be turned into an estimated 1RM like the example above. The guide [what is a PR in the gym](https://loadpr.com/guide/what-is-a-pr/) covers rep PRs and weight PRs in full.

### What LoadPR calls your current PR

In the LoadPR app, the current PR of a lift is the heaviest weight you have logged for it, at any number of reps. It is not an estimate: if your heaviest bench entry is 225 lb for 3, your current PR is 225 lb. The app estimates the 1RM separately with the Epley formula, which it writes as weight × (1 + 0.0333 × reps), so 200 lb for 3 reps comes to an estimated 219.98 lb. With LoadPR+ the estimate appears as its own line on the full progress chart. The percentage wheel works from your current PR or from any weight you type, so you can type your 1RM if you want percentages of it. More in [PR tracking](https://loadpr.com/features/pr-tracking/).

### Why programs use a percentage of your 1RM

Percentages let one plan fit every lifter. A program that says 80% gives a 140 kg squatter and a 60 kg squatter the same effort. For a 140 kg 1RM:

| % of 1RM | Exact | Loadable with kilo plates |
|---|---|---|
| 90% | 126 kg | 125 kg |
| 80% | 112 kg | 112.5 kg |
| 70% | 98 kg | 97.5 kg |
| 60% | 84 kg | 85 kg |

The exact number is rarely loadable, so you round to the nearest weight your plates can make. The [1RM percentage calculator](https://loadpr.com/1rm-percentage-calculator/) does that for the whole table.

### Every lift has its own 1RM

Your squat, bench press, deadlift and overhead press each have a separate 1RM, and so do variations such as a paused bench or a front squat. Keep them apart in your log. A 1RM also belongs to its conditions: a max with a belt and a max without one are different numbers, and so is a max in kg compared with one rounded to pounds.

### Mistakes with a 1RM

- **Counting a rep that was not a full rep.** A squat above depth or a bench that bounced is not a 1RM.
- **Estimating from very long sets.** A set of 15 says more about endurance than about your max.
- **Mixing formulas.** Epley and other formulas give slightly different estimates. Pick one and stay with it so your numbers compare. [How 1RM is calculated](https://loadpr.com/guide/how-to-calculate-1rm/) sets them side by side.
- **Training from an old max.** A 1RM from months ago may be too high or too low now. Re-estimate from a recent set.
- **Treating the estimate as a target.** An estimated 1RM is a planning number, not a weight you have to hit.

### Sources

- [One-repetition maximum: estimation formulas (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-repetition_maximum)

### FAQ

**What does 1RM stand for?**
One-repetition maximum: the heaviest weight you can lift for one full rep with good form.

**Is 1 RPM the same as 1RM?**
Yes. 1 RPM is a common way of typing 1RM. Both mean the most weight you can lift once.

**How do you estimate a 1RM without maxing out?**
Lift a weight for 3 to 5 reps and put it into a formula. By Epley, 100 kg for 5 reps is an estimated 1RM of 116.67 kg.

**Is a 1RM the same as a PR?**
A 1RM you have actually lifted is your 1-rep PR. A PR can also be for more reps, such as your best set of 5, which is a rep PR rather than a 1RM.

**What is 80% of a 140 kg 1RM?**
112 kg. With standard kilo plates on a 20 kg bar, the nearest loadable weight is 112.5 kg.

---

## What is a PR in the gym?

URL: https://loadpr.com/guide/what-is-a-pr/

Updated 2026-10-25

**Short answer: PR stands for personal record, the best you have ever done on a lift.** In the weight room it usually means the heaviest weight you have lifted for a given number of reps. Some lifters say PB, for personal best; it means the same. To “hit a PR” is to beat your old best.

### Example: reading PRs from a bench press log

Here are a lifter’s best bench press sets:

| Set | What it is |
|---|---|
| 225 lb × 1 | Weight PR (the heaviest weight lifted) |
| 205 lb × 3 | 3-rep PR |
| 185 lb × 5 | 5-rep PR |

Asked “what is your bench PR?”, this lifter says 225 lb, the heaviest weight on the list. Asked for a 5-rep PR, the answer is 185 lb. Each rep count has its own record.

### Weight PR vs rep PR

A **weight PR** is the heaviest weight you have lifted on a lift, at any reps. Most of the time that is a single. A **rep PR** is the heaviest weight for a set number of reps, or the most reps with a set weight: 185 lb for 6 beats 185 lb for 5. Rep PRs come much more often than weight PRs, which makes them a good way to see progress between heavy days.

### How to find your PR

Look back through your log for the lift and find the heaviest weight. That is your PR, and the reps next to it say which kind it is. If you have no log, your PR is the heaviest weight you are sure you lifted with full reps. Write down the conditions too, such as belt, paused or competition, because a paused bench and a touch-and-go bench are not the same lift.

### Gym PRs and meet PRs

Lifters who compete often keep two sets of records. A gym PR is the best you have done in training, judged by you. A meet PR, sometimes called a competition PR, is the best you have done on the platform, where judges decide whether the lift counts, the commands have to be followed and the bar is loaded with competition collars. Keep them apart in your log so neither one hides the other.

### PR vs 1RM

A 1-rep PR is a max you actually lifted. A rep PR also points to a one-rep max you have not tested yet: by the Epley formula, the 205 lb triple above comes to an estimated 225.5 lb, about the same as the 225 lb single. What a 1RM is and how it is estimated is covered in [what is a 1RM](https://loadpr.com/guide/what-is-1rm/).

### How LoadPR records your PRs

In the LoadPR app each lift keeps a list of PR entries, newest first. An entry holds the weight in lb or kg, the reps from 1 to 20, the date and an optional note. The current PR of the lift is the heaviest weight you have logged, at any reps; when two entries weigh the same, the newer one counts. Entries can be in different units, and LoadPR compares them by their real weight, so a 100 kg single (220.46 lb) counts as heavier than a 220 lb single.

The free version tracks up to 5 exercises, each with every PR you log. See [PR tracking](https://loadpr.com/features/pr-tracking/) for the details, including logging a PR with Siri.

### Mistakes when counting a PR

- **Leaving out the reps.** “205” says little on its own. 205 for 3 and 205 for 1 are different records.
- **Counting a rep that did not count.** A half squat or a bench with a big bounce is not a PR.
- **Comparing different lifts.** A paused bench, a belted squat or a sumo deadlift each deserve their own records.
- **Mixing kg and lb.** 100 kg is 220.46 lb, so it beats 220 lb. Convert before you compare, or use the [kg to lb converter](https://loadpr.com/kg-to-lb/).
- **Chasing a PR every session.** Records come from steady training, and most sessions are not record days.

### Sources

- [Personal record (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_record)

### FAQ

**What does PR mean in the gym?**
PR means personal record: the heaviest weight you have lifted on a lift for a given number of reps, such as a 225 lb bench single.

**What is my PR?**
Your PR is the heaviest weight you have lifted on that lift with full reps. If your best bench sets are 225 lb for 1 and 205 lb for 3, your bench PR is 225 lb.

**What is a rep PR?**
The heaviest weight for a set number of reps, or the most reps with a set weight. 185 lb for 6 is a rep PR over 185 lb for 5.

**Is a PR the same as a PB?**
Yes. PB means personal best and PR means personal record; both name your best lift, such as 225 lb for 1.

**What is a weight PR?**
The heaviest weight you have lifted on a lift at any reps. In a log with 225 lb for 1 and 205 lb for 3, the weight PR is 225 lb.

---

## How is 1RM calculated?

URL: https://loadpr.com/guide/how-to-calculate-1rm/

Updated 2026-10-25

**Short answer: a 1RM is calculated by putting a set you lifted for a few reps into a formula that estimates your one-rep max.** The four common formulas are Epley, Brzycki, Lombardi and O'Conner. For 100 kg lifted 5 times they give 116.67, 112.5, 117.46 and 112.5 kg. They agree closely at low reps and drift apart as the reps go up.

### Example: one set of 5, four formulas

Say you squat 100 kg for 5 reps. Here is each formula worked through for that set:

| Formula | Equation | 100 kg for 5 reps |
|---|---|---|
| Epley | weight × (1 + reps ÷ 30) | 100 × (1 + 5 ÷ 30) = 116.67 kg |
| Brzycki | weight × 36 ÷ (37 − reps) | 100 × 36 ÷ 32 = 112.5 kg |
| Lombardi | weight × reps to the power 0.1 | 100 × 5 to the power 0.1 = 117.46 kg |
| O'Conner | weight × (1 + reps ÷ 40) | 100 × (1 + 5 ÷ 40) = 112.5 kg |

So the estimate for this one set lands between 112.5 and 117.46 kg, depending on the formula. None of them is wrong: each is a different fit to how many reps people manage as the weight gets heavier. To run your own set through all four at once, use the [1RM calculator](https://loadpr.com/1rm-calculator/).

### Why the formulas split apart above about 10 reps

Here is the same 100 kg lifted for 10 and 15 reps:

| Formula | 10 reps | 15 reps |
|---|---|---|
| Epley | 133.33 kg | 150 kg |
| Brzycki | 133.33 kg | 163.64 kg |
| Lombardi | 125.89 kg | 131.1 kg |
| O'Conner | 125 kg | 137.5 kg |

At 5 reps the four answers stay between 112.5 and 117.46 kg. At 15 reps they run from 131.1 kg (Lombardi) to 163.64 kg (Brzycki). Brzycki climbs fastest because its divisor, 37 minus the reps, shrinks as the reps rise. Lombardi climbs slowest because a power of 0.1 grows very little. Epley and O'Conner add a fixed share per rep, one thirtieth and one fortieth.

The bigger reason is the lifter. A long set tests endurance as much as strength, and two people with the same max can get very different rep counts with the same weight. Every formula is an average, and the further a set is from a single, the less any average says about you.

### Picking one formula and keeping it

Epley and Brzycki are the most widely used, and at 10 reps they give the same answer: 133.33 kg for 100 kg. Below 10 reps Brzycki is the more cautious of the two; above 10 it is the more generous. Whichever you choose, the habits below matter more than the choice:

- **Use a hard set of about 3 to 5 reps.** Low-rep sets give the closest estimates.
- **Count only full reps.** A rep cut short or helped by a spotter inflates the result.
- **Stay with the same formula.** Your estimates then compare from month to month, even if the formula is a little high or low for you.

### The formulas run backwards: rep max charts

A 1RM formula also works the other way. Instead of turning a set into a max, it turns a max into the share of it you can lift for each rep count. By Epley, 5 reps is about 85.7% of a 1RM. That is what a [rep max chart](https://loadpr.com/guide/rep-max-chart/) lists, from 1 to 12 reps.

### Estimate or test?

An estimate costs nothing: it comes from a set you were doing anyway. A test gives the real number for that day, but it takes a full session, careful warm-ups and a spotter or safety arms. Most lifters estimate between tests and test now and then, for example at the end of a training block. When you do test, [how to test your 1RM safely](https://loadpr.com/guide/how-to-test-your-1rm/) walks through the attempts.

### How LoadPR estimates your 1RM

The LoadPR app estimates a 1RM from your logged sets with the Epley formula by default. With LoadPR+ you can pick another formula, such as Brzycki, and the estimate appears as its own line on the full progress chart. The app keeps your current PR separate from the estimate: the current PR is the heaviest weight you have logged, not a formula result. More in [PR tracking](https://loadpr.com/features/pr-tracking/).

### Mistakes when calculating a 1RM

- **Estimating from a set of 12 or more.** At 15 reps the formulas are more than 30 kg apart for a 100 kg set.
- **Using a set that was not close to failure.** If you could have done 3 more reps, the formula underestimates you.
- **Switching formulas between months.** A jump from 112.5 to 117.46 kg can be the formula, not your strength.
- **Mixing units.** Estimate in the unit you lifted in, then convert if you need to.
- **Treating the estimate as a weight to hit.** It is a planning number for setting training loads.

### Sources

- [One-repetition maximum: estimation formulas (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-repetition_maximum)

### FAQ

**What is the most accurate 1RM formula?**
No formula is right for everyone. Epley and Brzycki are the most used and agree closely at low reps: for 100 kg lifted 5 times they give 116.67 kg and 112.5 kg.

**What is the Epley formula?**
1RM = weight × (1 + reps ÷ 30). For 100 kg lifted 5 times it estimates a 1RM of 116.67 kg.

**What is the Brzycki formula?**
1RM = weight × 36 ÷ (37 − reps). For 100 kg lifted 5 times it estimates a 1RM of 112.5 kg.

**Why do 1RM formulas give different answers?**
Each one is a different fit to how reps drop as the weight rises. For 100 kg lifted 10 times, O'Conner gives 125 kg and Epley gives 133.33 kg.

**How many reps give the best 1RM estimate?**
A hard set of about 3 to 5 reps. At 15 reps the four common formulas spread from 131.1 kg to 163.64 kg for a 100 kg set.

---

## What percentage of your 1RM can you lift for each rep count?

URL: https://loadpr.com/guide/rep-max-chart/

Updated 2026-10-25

**Short answer: a rep max chart turns a rep count into a percentage of your 1RM.** By the Epley formula you can lift about 85.7% of your 1RM for 5 reps and 75% for 10. By Brzycki, 5 reps is 88.9% and 10 reps is also 75%. A single is 100% by definition.

### Example: sets of 5 from a 140 kg max

Your squat max is 140 kg and the plan calls for a hard set of 5. The chart gives 85.7% for 5 reps by Epley:

- 140 × 85.7% = 119.98 kg
- With kilo plates on a 20 kg bar, the nearest loads are **120 kg** (25 + 25 on each side) and 117.5 kg below it.

For a 315 lb bench max the same row gives 315 × 85.7% = 269.96 lb. The nearest loads are **270 lb** (45, 45, 10, 10 and 2.5 on each side) and 265 lb. For any other max, the [1RM percentage calculator](https://loadpr.com/1rm-percentage-calculator/) does the multiplying and the rounding.

### Rep max chart, 1 to 12 reps

The percentage of your 1RM you can lift for each number of reps, taken to the last rep you can complete:

| Reps | Epley | Brzycki |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 100% | 100% |
| 2 | 93.7% | 97.2% |
| 3 | 90.9% | 94.4% |
| 4 | 88.2% | 91.7% |
| 5 | 85.7% | 88.9% |
| 6 | 83.3% | 86.1% |
| 7 | 81.1% | 83.3% |
| 8 | 78.9% | 80.6% |
| 9 | 76.9% | 77.8% |
| 10 | 75% | 75% |
| 11 | 73.2% | 72.2% |
| 12 | 71.4% | 69.4% |

The chart stops at 12 reps because past that point the formulas disagree more and more, and a percentage says little about a set of 15 or 20.

### How to read the chart

Find the number of reps you plan to do, read the percentage across, and multiply it by your 1RM. Then round to a weight your plates can make. The chart describes a set taken to the last rep you can manage. If your program wants reps left in the tank, use a lower percentage than the chart shows for that rep count.

The chart is a 1RM formula run backwards. The guide [how 1RM is calculated](https://loadpr.com/guide/how-to-calculate-1rm/) shows the formulas themselves.

### Epley vs Brzycki on the chart

The two columns meet at 10 reps, where both say 75%. Below 10 reps Brzycki gives the higher percentage, so it expects you to handle more weight for the same reps. Above 10 it gives the lower one. For the 5-rep example the difference looks like this:

| 5 reps from a | Epley (85.7%) | Brzycki (88.9%) |
|---|---|---|
| 140 kg max | 119.98 kg, load 120 kg | 124.46 kg, load 125 kg |
| 315 lb max | 269.96 lb, load 270 lb | 280.04 lb, load 280 lb |

Neither column is the true one. If the Epley weights feel easy for you at 5 reps, the Brzycki column may fit you better, and the other way round. Pick the one that matches what you actually do in training and stay with it.

### Why a single is 100%

A one-rep max is the weight you can lift once, so 1 rep is 100% of it in every column. The Epley equation, taken literally, puts a single slightly above the weight lifted: 100 kg for 1 rep comes to 103.33 kg. This chart does not use that row, and fixes 1 rep at 100%.

If you want a real number for the top of the chart instead of an estimate, [how to test your 1RM safely](https://loadpr.com/guide/how-to-test-your-1rm/) lays out a test day.

### Mistakes with a rep max chart

- **Treating the percentages as exact.** They are averages. Your own rep counts at 85% may be one or two off.
- **Using a max that is out of date.** A percentage of an old 1RM gives old weights.
- **Forgetting to round.** 119.98 kg cannot go on the bar; 120 kg can.
- **Mixing units.** Take the percentage of a kg max in kg, and of a lb max in lb.
- **Reading the chart for every set.** The chart is for sets to the last rep. Most working sets stop short of that.

### Sources

- [One-repetition maximum: estimation formulas (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-repetition_maximum)

### FAQ

**What percentage of 1RM is 5 reps?**
About 85.7% by Epley and 88.9% by Brzycki. For a 140 kg max that is 119.98 kg by Epley, so load 120 kg.

**What percentage of 1RM is 10 reps?**
75% by both Epley and Brzycki. For a 315 lb max that is 236.25 lb, so load 235 lb or 240 lb.

**What percentage of 1RM is 3 reps?**
About 90.9% by Epley and 94.4% by Brzycki. A set of 3 sits close to your max.

**What percentage of 1RM is 8 reps?**
About 78.9% by Epley and 80.6% by Brzycki, a little under four fifths of your max.

**Why is 1 rep 100% on a rep max chart?**
A single at your max is your 1RM by definition, so 1 rep is 100% in every column, even though Epley's equation would give 103.33 kg for 100 kg lifted once.

---

## How do you test your 1RM safely?

URL: https://loadpr.com/guide/how-to-test-your-1rm/

Updated 2026-10-25

**Short answer: warm up, then work up to your max in jumps that get smaller as the bar gets heavier, with a spotter or safety arms in place.** A simple progression is 50%, 70%, 80%, 90% and 95% of the max you plan to hit, then 100%. For a planned 140 kg squat that is 70, 97.5, 112.5, 125, 132.5 and 140 kg.

### Example: a test day for a 140 kg squat

Pick a planned max first: a recent best single, or an estimate from a hard set of 3 to 5 (see [how 1RM is calculated](https://loadpr.com/guide/how-to-calculate-1rm/)). Then take each percentage of it and round to a weight your plates can make:

| Set | % of planned max | Weight | Reps |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 50% | 70 kg | 5 |
| 2 | 70% | 97.5 kg | 3 |
| 3 | 80% | 112.5 kg | 1 |
| 4 | 90% | 125 kg | 1 |
| 5 | 95% | 132.5 kg | 1 |
| 6 | 100% | 140 kg | 1 |

The exact 70% of 140 kg is 98 kg, and 97.5 kg is the nearest weight with kilo plates on a 20 kg bar. Every row is rounded the same way. The reps are a common pattern: a few reps while the bar is light, then singles so you save your energy for the top.

### Example: a test day for a 315 lb bench press

The same percentages of a planned 315 lb max, rounded to weights you can load with pound plates on a 45 lb bar:

| Set | % of planned max | Weight | Reps |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 50% | 160 lb | 5 |
| 2 | 70% | 220 lb | 3 |
| 3 | 80% | 250 lb | 1 |
| 4 | 90% | 285 lb | 1 |
| 5 | 95% | 300 lb | 1 |
| 6 | 100% | 315 lb | 1 |

The top attempt is three 45 lb plates on each side of the bar. To see the plates for any of the other sets, enter the weight in the [plate calculator](https://loadpr.com/plate-calculator/).

### Before you test

- **Come in rested.** Test after a lighter week or at the end of a training block, not after a hard session.
- **Decide what counts.** Squat depth, a pause on the chest for the bench, lockout on the deadlift. Hold every attempt to the same standard you will use next time.
- **Use the same setup.** Belt or no belt, the same bar and the same unit. A max belongs to its conditions.
- **Warm up your body before the bar.** A few minutes of easy movement, then the first set of the table.

### Safety: spotters, safety arms and missing a rep

A heavy single can fail without warning, so plan the miss before you lift.

- **Squat inside a rack** with the safety arms set just below the bottom of your squat. If you miss, sit down onto them.
- **Bench with a spotter** who knows when to take the bar, or with safety arms set just below your chest. Never test a bench max alone without them.
- **On the deadlift**, a miss is simply putting the bar down. Keep the area around the platform clear.
- **Stop if something hurts.** A sharp pain is a reason to end the session, not to take the next attempt.

### Choosing the last jump

The 95% single tells you a lot. If it moved fast, take your planned max. If it was slow or your form slipped, stop there or take a smaller final jump, and count the 95% single as the day's result. If you miss the max, try it once more at most; a third try at the same weight rarely goes better than the second.

### After the test

A max you lifted is your 1-rep PR for that lift. In the LoadPR app, log it as an entry with 1 rep: if it is your heaviest entry for the lift, it becomes your current PR, and the percentage wheel can work from it. See [PR tracking](https://loadpr.com/features/pr-tracking/). To set training weights from your new max for other rep counts, use the [rep max chart](https://loadpr.com/guide/rep-max-chart/).

### Mistakes on test day

- **Too many warm-up reps.** Sets of 5 near the top tire you before the single that matters.
- **A big last jump.** Going from 90% straight to a new max is how attempts get missed.
- **No plan for a miss.** Set the safety arms or brief the spotter before the first heavy single, not after.
- **Changing the standard.** A higher squat or a bounced bench gives a bigger number that you cannot repeat.
- **Testing too often.** Between tests, estimate your max from a hard set instead.

### FAQ

**How do you warm up for a 1RM test?**
Work up through lighter sets to singles. For a planned 140 kg squat: 70 kg for 5, 97.5 kg for 3, then singles at 112.5, 125 and 132.5 kg before 140 kg.

**How many sets does a 1RM test take?**
In this pattern, six: 50%, 70%, 80%, 90% and 95% of the planned max, then 100%. For a 315 lb plan that ends 285, 300 and 315 lb.

**What should my last warm-up be before a 315 lb max?**
95% of 315 lb is 299.25 lb, so load 300 lb (45, 45, 35 and 2.5 on each side), then take 315 lb.

**Should I test my 1RM or estimate it?**
Estimate between tests and test now and then. 100 kg for 5 reps already gives an estimated 116.67 kg by Epley without a max attempt.

**Do I need a spotter to test my 1RM?**
For the bench press, yes, or safety arms set just below your chest. Even the 90% single of a 140 kg plan, 125 kg, can stall without warning.

---

## How many warm-up sets before squat, bench and deadlift?

URL: https://loadpr.com/guide/warm-up-sets/

Updated 2026-10-25

**Short answer: most lifters do 3 to 5 warm-up sets before a heavy squat, bench press or deadlift, and more as the work set gets heavier.** A simple ramp is four sets: 40% of your work set for 5 reps, 60% for 5, 75% for 3 and 85% for 2. Before 315 lb that is 125, 190, 235 and 270 lb. Before 140 kg it is 55, 85, 105 and 120 kg.

### Example: warming up for 315 lb

Your top set today is 315 lb. Take each percentage of 315 lb and round it to the nearest 5 lb, a weight you can load with pound plates on a 45 lb bar:

| Step | Weight × reps | Plates on each side |
|---|---|---|
| 40% | 125 lb × 5 | 35, 5 |
| 60% | 190 lb × 5 | 45, 25, 2.5 |
| 75% | 235 lb × 3 | 45, 45, 5 |
| 85% | 270 lb × 2 | 45, 45, 10, 10, 2.5 |
| Work set | 315 lb | 45, 45, 45 |

The exact 40% of 315 lb is 126 lb and the exact 85% is 267.75 lb; every row is rounded the same way. The [warmup calculator](https://loadpr.com/warmup-calculator/) builds this ramp for any work weight in lb or kg.

### Example: warming up for 140 kg

The same ramp before a 140 kg top set, rounded to the nearest 2.5 kg for kilo plates on a 20 kg bar:

| Step | Weight × reps | Plates on each side |
|---|---|---|
| 40% | 55 kg × 5 | 15, 2.5 |
| 60% | 85 kg × 5 | 25, 5, 2.5 |
| 75% | 105 kg × 3 | 25, 15, 2.5 |
| 85% | 120 kg × 2 | 25, 25 |
| Work set | 140 kg | 25, 25, 10 |

Here the exact values are 56, 84, 105 and 119 kg. Rounding moves each set by 1 kg at most, which makes no difference to how the warm-up feels.

### Why the reps drop as the weight rises

Warm-up sets get you ready for the work set; they should not tire you before it. The light sets get more reps because they cost almost nothing and let you practise the movement. Near the top the reps drop to 3 and then 2, so you feel a heavy bar in your hands without spending the energy the work set needs. The jumps in this ramp stay between 10 and 20 percentage points: 40 to 60, 60 to 75, 75 to 85, then 85 to 100.

### Squat, bench press and deadlift

- **Squat.** Hips, knees and ankles all have to move through a full range, so many lifters do a set or two with the empty bar before the first loaded set. The ramp then works as written.
- **Bench press.** The shoulders and elbows take the load. Touch the chest on every warm-up rep the same way you will on the work set, so the groove is set before the weight is heavy.
- **Deadlift.** The bar starts on the floor, and an empty bar sits too low to pull from with a normal setup. Most lifters start with one full-size plate on each side: 135 lb with 45 lb plates or 60 kg with 20 kg plates. Before a 315 lb deadlift, the 40% step (125 lb) is lighter than that, so start at 135 lb and go on to 190, 235 and 270 lb.

### Light and heavy work sets

The right number of warm-up sets follows the work weight. For a light work set, the first steps fall at or near the empty bar. Before 95 lb the ramp gives 40, 55, 70 and 80 lb, and 40 lb is less than a 45 lb bar, so use the bar for that step. Before 60 kg it gives 25, 35, 45 and 50 kg, and 25 kg is only 5 kg over a 20 kg bar. Two or three sets are plenty there.

For a heavy work set the gap at the top grows. From 85% to the work set is 45 lb (270 to 315 lb) or 20 kg (120 to 140 kg). That is fine for a set of several reps. Before a heavy single or a max attempt, add singles above 85%; [how to test your 1RM safely](https://loadpr.com/guide/how-to-test-your-1rm/) lays them out.

### Loading each warm-up set

Every warm-up set is a new weight to load, which is where most of the plate math in a session happens. The [plate calculator](https://loadpr.com/plate-calculator/) shows the plates on each side for any of the weights above. The LoadPR app does not plan warm-up sets for you. You type a weight and it draws one side of the bar with the plates to put on, so you can enter each warm-up weight in turn. More in [plate loading](https://loadpr.com/features/plate-loading/).

### Mistakes with warm-up sets

- **Too many reps near the top.** Sets of 5 or more at 85% tire you before the set that matters.
- **One big jump.** Going from the empty bar straight to the work set skips the practice at a heavy weight.
- **Taking the percentages from your 1RM.** This ramp is a percentage of today's work set, not of your max.
- **Loading the exact number.** 126 lb cannot be made with standard pound plates on a 45 lb bar; 125 lb can.
- **The same warm-up for every lift.** A deadlift starts from a plate on each side, not from the empty bar.

### FAQ

**How many warm-up sets should I do?**
Usually 3 to 5. A simple ramp is four: 40%, 60%, 75% and 85% of the work set. Before 315 lb that is 125, 190, 235 and 270 lb.

**How many warm-up sets before a 140 kg squat?**
Four loaded sets in this ramp, after the empty bar if you like: 55 kg for 5, 85 kg for 5, 105 kg for 3 and 120 kg for 2.

**How should I warm up for deadlifts?**
Start with one full-size plate on each side, 135 lb or 60 kg, then ramp. Before 315 lb that means 135, 190, 235 and 270 lb.

**Do warm-up sets count as working sets?**
No. They prepare you for the work set and should leave you fresh. The last one in this ramp is 85% for 2: 270 lb before a 315 lb set.

**How many reps should each warm-up set have?**
Fewer as the bar gets heavier. This ramp uses 5, 5, 3 and 2 reps at 40%, 60%, 75% and 85% of the work set.

---

## What is the training max in 5/3/1?

URL: https://loadpr.com/guide/531-training-max/

Updated 2026-10-28

**Short answer: in 5/3/1 the training max (TM) is 90% of your 1RM, and every percentage in the program is taken from the training max, not from your max.** A 455 lb deadlift max gives a 409.5 lb training max, so the 85% set is 350 lb, not 386.75 lb. Later versions of Jim Wendler's program often set the training max at 85% of the 1RM instead.

### Example: the 85% set from a 455 lb deadlift

Your deadlift max is 455 lb and week 1 calls for a top set at 85%. Work it out in three steps:

- Take 90% of the 1RM: 455 × 90% = **409.5 lb**. That is your training max.
- Take the week's percentage of the training max: 409.5 × 85% = 348.08 lb.
- Round to a weight you can load: **350 lb**, which is three 45s, a 10, a 5 and a 2.5 on each side of a 45 lb bar.

Taking 85% of the 455 lb max directly gives 386.75 lb. The arithmetic is fine, but the base is wrong: 5/3/1 never asks for a percentage of your true max. That is why its weights look lower than many lifters expect.

### Every 5/3/1 week from a 409.5 lb training max

The original program runs four weeks. The last set of weeks 1 to 3 is a plus set: as many good reps as you can. Each weight below is the percentage of the 409.5 lb training max, rounded to the nearest load with pound plates on a 45 lb bar:

| Week | Set 1 | Set 2 | Set 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (5s) | 65% × 5: 265 lb | 75% × 5: 305 lb | 85% × 5+: 350 lb |
| 2 (3s) | 70% × 3: 285 lb | 80% × 3: 330 lb | 90% × 3+: 370 lb |
| 3 (5/3/1) | 75% × 5: 305 lb | 85% × 3: 350 lb | 95% × 1+: 390 lb |
| 4 (deload) | 40% × 5: 165 lb | 50% × 5: 205 lb | 60% × 5: 245 lb |

The heaviest set of the cycle, 95% in week 3, is 389.03 lb exact and 390 lb on the bar, still well under the 455 lb max. That is the point: the training max keeps every set submaximal so you can add weight cycle after cycle. For any other max, the [5/3/1 calculator](https://loadpr.com/531-calculator/) builds all four weeks from your 1RM, with the plates for every set.

### Training max at 90% or 85%?

The original 5/3/1 uses 90% of your 1RM. Wendler's later books often recommend 85%, which lowers every set and leaves more reps in each plus set. The same 455 lb max under both:

|  | TM at 90% | TM at 85% |
|---|---|---|
| Training max | 409.5 lb | 386.75 lb |
| Week 1, 85% set | 348.08 lb, load 350 lb | 328.74 lb, load 330 lb |
| Week 2, 90% set | 368.55 lb, load 370 lb | 348.08 lb, load 350 lb |
| Week 3, 95% set | 389.03 lb, load 390 lb | 367.41 lb, load 365 lb |

Use the percentage your version of the program is written for. If the 90% version leaves you grinding out the minimum reps on the plus sets, 85% is the more conservative choice.

### Training max vs 1RM

A [1RM](https://loadpr.com/guide/what-is-1rm/) is the heaviest weight you can lift once. A training max is a planning number set below it on purpose. You never test the training max and you are not meant to lift it for a single; it only exists so the program's percentages land on weights you can handle for the prescribed reps. Your 1RM can go up while the training max climbs slowly and steadily, and that gap is by design.

### How to calculate your training max without testing

You don't need a fresh max-out. Estimate the 1RM from a hard set of 3 to 5 reps, then take 90% of the estimate. Say you deadlift 385 lb for 5:

- Epley estimate: 385 × (1 + 5 ÷ 30) = **449.17 lb**
- Training max: 449.17 × 90% = **404.25 lb**

The [1RM calculator](https://loadpr.com/1rm-calculator/) gives the estimate from any set, and [how 1RM is calculated](https://loadpr.com/guide/how-to-calculate-1rm/) compares the formulas.

### How much to add to the training max each cycle

After each cycle the original program adds 5 lb (2.5 kg) to the training max for the bench press and overhead press, and 10 lb (5 kg) for the squat and deadlift. The weight goes on the training max itself, not on your 1RM. If you add it to the 1RM and recompute 90%, the training max grows by less than the planned amount each cycle.

| Deadlift | Training max | Week 1, 85% set |
|---|---|---|
| Cycle 1 | 409.5 lb | 348.08 lb, load 350 lb |
| Cycle 2 (+10 lb) | 419.5 lb | 356.58 lb, load 355 lb |

### The same in kilos: a 140 kg squat

A 140 kg squat max gives a training max of 140 × 90% = **126 kg**. Rounded to kilo plates on a 20 kg bar:

| Week | Set 1 | Set 2 | Set 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 65%: 82.5 kg | 75%: 95 kg | 85%: 107.5 kg |
| 2 | 70%: 87.5 kg | 80%: 100 kg | 90%: 112.5 kg |
| 3 | 75%: 95 kg | 85%: 107.5 kg | 95%: 120 kg |

With the training max at 85% instead, it is 119 kg. Next cycle the squat training max goes up 5 kg, from 126 to 131 kg, and the week 1 top set moves from 107.1 kg exact (load 107.5 kg) to 111.35 kg exact (load 112.5 kg).

### Loading 5/3/1 sets in LoadPR

LoadPR does not plan 5/3/1 cycles for you, but its percentage wheel works from any weight you type, not only from a logged PR. Type your training max, turn the wheel to the week's percentage and it shows a weight you can load with the plates for one side of the bar. The wheel runs from 50% to 120% in 5% steps, so for the 40% deload set use the [plate calculator](https://loadpr.com/plate-calculator/). More in [percentages of your PR](https://loadpr.com/features/percentages/).

### Mistakes with the training max

- **Taking percentages from the 1RM.** 85% of a 455 lb max is 386.75 lb; the program wants 85% of the 409.5 lb training max, 350 lb.
- **Adding the cycle increase to the 1RM.** Add 5 or 10 lb to the training max itself.
- **Setting the training max from an old or hopeful max.** A too-high training max makes the plus sets grind. Use a recent max or an estimate from a hard set.
- **Loading the exact number.** 348.08 lb can't go on a bar; 350 lb can.
- **Mixing units.** Keep the max, the training max and the sets in the same unit.

### Sources

- [Jim Wendler, “5/3/1 for a Beginner” (JimWendler.com)](https://www.jimwendler.com/blogs/jimwendler-com/101065094-5-3-1-for-a-beginner)

### FAQ

**What is a training max in 5/3/1?**
A planning number set below your 1RM, 90% of it in the original program. All the program's percentages come from it: a 455 lb max gives a 409.5 lb training max.

**Is the 5/3/1 training max 90% or 85%?**
The original program uses 90%; Wendler's later books often use 85%. For a 455 lb max that is 409.5 lb or 386.75 lb.

**How do you calculate your training max?**
Multiply your 1RM by 0.9. Without a tested max, estimate one first: 385 lb for 5 reps is about 449.17 lb by Epley, so the training max is 404.25 lb.

**Why are my 5/3/1 weights lower than expected?**
The percentages are of the training max, not your 1RM. From a 455 lb max the week 1 85% set is 350 lb, not 386.75 lb.

**How much do you add to the 5/3/1 training max each cycle?**
5 lb (2.5 kg) for bench and press, 10 lb (5 kg) for squat and deadlift, added to the training max: 409.5 lb becomes 419.5 lb.

---

## Why can't I load an exact weight on a barbell?

URL: https://loadpr.com/guide/cant-load-exact-weight/

Updated 2026-10-28

**Short answer: every plate goes on both sides of the bar, so the total can only move in steps of twice your smallest plate: 5 lb steps with 2.5 lb plates, and 2.5 kg steps with 1.25 kg plates.** A target like 172 lb falls between 170 lb and 175 lb, and no mix of standard plates makes it. You load the nearest weight you can build, or add smaller plates.

### Example: 80% of a 215 lb max

Your program calls for 80% of a 215 lb squat. Work it out:

- 215 × 80% = **172 lb**.
- Take off the 45 lb bar: 127 lb of plates, so 63.5 lb on each side.
- The smallest standard plate is 2.5 lb, so each side can hold 62.5 lb or 65 lb, never 63.5 lb.

The two loads you can build are **170 lb** (a 45, a 10, a 5 and a 2.5 on each side) and **175 lb** (a 45 and two 10s on each side). 170 lb is 2 lb under the target and 175 lb is 3 lb over, so 170 lb is the nearest loadable weight.

### The smallest jump is two of your smallest plates

Whatever plates you own, the smallest change you can make to the bar is one of your lightest plates on each side:

| Smallest plate | Smallest jump | Example loads |
|---|---|---|
| 5 lb | 10 lb | 185, 195 lb |
| 2.5 lb | 5 lb | 170, 175 lb |
| 1.25 lb | 2.5 lb | 170, 172.5 lb |
| 1 lb | 2 lb | 185, 187 lb |
| 1.25 kg | 2.5 kg | 100, 102.5 kg |
| 0.5 kg | 1 kg | 101, 102 kg |

So the question is never whether a number is "odd", only whether it sits on one of your steps. On a 45 lb bar with standard pound plates, every loadable total ends in 0 or 5.

### Nearest loadable weight for common targets

Targets from percentages and programs, with the loads just below and just above, using standard plates on a 45 lb or 20 kg bar:

| Target | Load below (per side) | Load above (per side) |
|---|---|---|
| 172 lb | 170 lb (45, 10, 5, 2.5) | 175 lb (45, 10, 10) |
| 186 lb | 185 lb (45, 25) | 190 lb (45, 25, 2.5) |
| 191.25 lb | 190 lb (45, 25, 2.5) | 195 lb (45, 25, 5) |
| 202.5 lb | 200 lb (45, 25, 5, 2.5) | 205 lb (45, 35) |
| 102 kg | 100 kg (25, 15) | 102.5 kg (25, 15, 1.25) |
| 133 kg | 132.5 kg (25, 25, 5, 1.25) | 135 kg (25, 25, 5, 2.5) |

191.25 lb and 202.5 lb are 85% and 90% of 225 lb, which shows how often percentages miss the steps. The [plate calculator](https://loadpr.com/plate-calculator/) lists both neighbors for any target, with the plates for each.

### Round up or round down?

Taking whichever load is closer is the simplest rule, and with standard plates it is never more than half a step off: 2.5 lb or 1.25 kg. When the target sits exactly in the middle, like 202.5 lb between 200 and 205, you have to choose:

- **Round down** on heavy top sets and anything near your max, where a few extra pounds can cost a rep.
- **Round up** on lighter work, such as warm-ups and back-off sets, if you would rather not undershoot.
- **Stay consistent.** If you always round the same way, week-to-week progress in your log still compares like with like.

The [closest loadable weight](https://loadpr.com/features/closest-loadable-weight/) page explains the rule the LoadPR app uses.

### No 2.5 lb plates in your gym

If the smallest plate on the rack is a 5, the bar moves in 10 lb steps. A 190 lb target with 45, 25, 10 and 5 lb plates can only be 185 lb (a 45 and a 25 on each side) or 195 lb (a 45, a 25 and a 5 on each side). That gap is why missing change plates hurt most on presses, where 10 lb is a big jump. The [home gym plate calculator](https://loadpr.com/home-gym-plate-calculator/) works from the plates you actually own, so it only shows loads you can build.

### Who has 1 lb plates? Microplates

Small plates under 2.5 lb, often called microplates or fractional plates, are the real fix. Sizes depend on the set; common ones include 1.25 lb, 1 lb and 0.5 lb, and 0.5 kg in kilos.

- With a pair of 1.25 lb plates, 172 lb becomes **172.5 lb**: a 35, a 25, a 2.5 and a 1.25 on each side.
- With a pair of 1 lb plates the step is 2 lb, so 186 lb still is not exact: the nearest loads are 185 lb and **187 lb** (a 45, a 25 and a 1 on each side). An exact 186 lb needs half a pound more on each side.
- In kilos, two 0.5 kg plates on each side make **102 kg** exactly: a 25, a 15 and two 0.5s on each side of a 20 kg bar.

For most lifts, rounding to the nearest step is fine. Microplates matter most when the jump between sessions is small compared with the weight, as on the overhead press and bench press.

### A kilo program in a pound gym

Programs written in kilos rarely land on pound steps. 100 kg is 220.46 lb, and the nearest loads on a 45 lb bar are **220 lb** (a 45, a 35, a 5 and a 2.5 on each side) and 225 lb (two 45s on each side). 220 lb is less than half a pound off, closer than any kilo-to-pound rule of thumb. Convert the weight first with the [kg to lb converter](https://loadpr.com/kg-to-lb/), then round to your plates, not to the nearest 5 or 10 in your head.

### Common mistakes

- **Halving the gap wrong.** To move the bar by 2 lb, each side needs 1 lb, not 2 lb.
- **Forgetting the bar.** Take the bar off the target before you split the plates between the sides.
- **Rounding before converting.** Convert kg to lb (or back) first, then round to your plates once; rounding twice stacks two errors.
- **Assuming the gym has every plate.** Without 2.5s or with only one pair, the steps get bigger. Count what is on the rack.
- **Chasing the exact number.** A 2 lb difference from the target is noise for most sets; load the nearest weight and lift.

### FAQ

**Why can't I load an exact weight on a barbell?**
Plates go on in pairs, so the total moves in steps of twice your smallest plate: 5 lb with 2.5 lb plates, 2.5 kg with 1.25 kg plates. 172 lb falls between 170 lb and 175 lb.

**What is the smallest jump you can make on a barbell?**
Two of your lightest plates: 5 lb with 2.5 lb plates, 2.5 lb with 1.25 lb microplates, 2.5 kg with 1.25 kg plates and 1 kg with 0.5 kg plates.

**Should I round a barbell weight up or down?**
Take the closer load. On a tie, such as 202.5 lb between 200 lb and 205 lb, round down for heavy sets near your max and stay consistent from week to week.

**Do 1 lb plates let me load any weight?**
No. A pair of 1 lb plates makes 2 lb steps, so 186 lb on a 45 lb bar becomes 185 lb or 187 lb. An exact 186 lb needs 0.5 lb more on each side.

**How do I load a 100 kg program weight with pound plates?**
100 kg is 220.46 lb. On a 45 lb bar the nearest load is 220 lb: a 45, a 35, a 5 and a 2.5 on each side.

---

## How do you count the weight on a barbell?

URL: https://loadpr.com/guide/count-weight-on-a-barbell/

Updated 2026-10-29

**Short answer: add up the plates on one side, double that, then add the bar.** A 45 lb bar with a 45, a 25 and a 5 on each side is 45 + 2 × (45 + 25 + 5) = 195 lb. A properly loaded bar carries the same plates on both ends, so you only need to read one side.

### Example: a 45, a 25 and a 5 on each side

You walk up to a bar in a pound gym and see three plates on the near end: a 45, a 25 and a 5. Count it in three steps:

- Plates on one side: 45 + 25 + 5 = 75 lb.
- Both sides: 2 × 75 = 150 lb.
- Add the bar: 150 + 45 = **195 lb**.

The order matters only for reading: the biggest plate sits closest to the middle of the bar, and the small ones are on the outside. Read from the inside out and say the numbers as you go.

### Counting in kilos

The rule is the same in a kilo gym, with a 20 kg bar. A 25, a 15 and a 5 on each side:

- One side: 25 + 15 + 5 = 45 kg.
- Both sides plus the bar: 20 + 2 × 45 = **110 kg**.

Different plates can make the same total: a 25 and a 20 on each side is also 110 kg. On a 15 kg women's bar the first set of plates makes 105 kg, so check which bar you have; [how much a barbell weighs](https://loadpr.com/guide/barbell-weights/) lists the common ones.

### Reading competition plates by color

On calibrated kilo plates the color tells you the weight before you can read the number: red 25 kg, blue 20 kg, yellow 15 kg, green 10 kg, white 5 kg. A red and a blue on each side of a 20 kg bar is 110 kg. At a meet, add the two 2.5 kg competition collars and it is **115 kg**. Pound bumpers sometimes borrow the same colors for different weights, so in a pound gym read the number on the plate. All the colors are in [Olympic plate colors](https://loadpr.com/guide/olympic-plate-colors/).

### Quick reference: one side to total

Standard plates on a 45 lb or 20 kg bar, no collars:

| One side (lb) | Total | One side (kg) | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| 45, 10 | 155 lb | 25, 15 | 100 kg |
| 45, 25 | 185 lb | 25, 15, 5 | 110 kg |
| 45, 25, 5 | 195 lb | 25, 20 | 110 kg |
| 45, 35 | 205 lb | 25, 25, 10 | 140 kg |
| 45, 25, 10 | 205 lb |  |  |
| 45, 45, 25 | 275 lb |  |  |

For bars loaded only with full plates (135, 225, 315, 405 lb), see [how much is 1 to 6 plates on each side](https://loadpr.com/guide/plates-on-each-side/).

### Kilo plates in a pound gym

Mixed units are where counting goes wrong. A 20 kg plate is 44.09 lb, not 45 lb, so convert every plate to one unit before you add. A 45 lb bar with one 20 kg plate on each side:

- In pounds: 45 + 2 × 44.09 = **133.18 lb**, not 135 lb.
- In kilos: the 45 lb bar is 20.41 kg, so 20.41 + 2 × 20 = **60.41 kg**.

[How much a plate weighs](https://loadpr.com/guide/how-much-does-a-plate-weigh/) lists every plate in both units, and the [kg to lb converter](https://loadpr.com/kg-to-lb/) handles the totals.

### Collars and the two sides

Spring clips weigh little and most lifters leave them out of the count. Competition collars weigh 2.5 kg each, so they add 5 kg to the bar; see [how much barbell collars weigh](https://loadpr.com/guide/barbell-collar-weight/). If the two sides are not loaded the same, do not double one side: add both sides separately, then the bar, and fix the bar before you lift, because an uneven bar tips toward the heavy end.

### Let a tool add it up

[What's on the bar](https://loadpr.com/whats-on-the-bar/) does this count for you: tap the plates you see on one side, pick the bar and collars, and it shows the total in kg and lb. To go the other way, from a target weight to the plates per side, use the [plate calculator](https://loadpr.com/plate-calculator/).

### Common mistakes

- **Forgetting the bar.** A 45, a 25 and a 5 on each side are 150 lb of plates; the bar makes it 195 lb.
- **Counting one side only.** Plates go on both ends, so each plate you see counts twice.
- **Assuming every bar weighs 45 lb.** A women's bar is 15 kg (33 lb), and specialty bars vary by model.
- **Treating a 20 kg plate as a 45.** A 20 kg plate is 44.09 lb, and over several plates the gap adds up.
- **Reading colors in a pound gym.** Bumper colors are not a standard there; trust the number stamped on the plate.

### FAQ

**How do you count the weight on a barbell?**
Add the plates on one side, double it and add the bar. A 45, a 25 and a 5 on each side of a 45 lb bar is 45 + 2 × 75 = 195 lb.

**How much weight is on the bar with a 45 and a 25 on each side?**
185 lb on a 45 lb bar: 45 + 2 × (45 + 25).

**How much is a red and a blue plate on each side?**
