110 kg on a 20 kg bar, since red is 25 kg and blue is 20 kg. With two 2.5 kg competition collars it is 115 kg.

**How do I count kg plates on a lb bar?**
Convert the plates first: a 20 kg plate is 44.09 lb, so one on each side of a 45 lb bar is 133.18 lb, not 135 lb.

# Tool variations

## How do you turn an AMRAP set into a 1RM?

URL: https://loadpr.com/1rm-calculator/amrap-to-1rm/

To estimate your max from an AMRAP set, put the weight and the number of full reps into a 1RM formula. 225 lb for 8 reps gives an estimated 1RM of 285 lb by Epley, which is 225 × (1 + 8 ÷ 30), and 279.31 lb by Brzycki. Enter your own set in the calculator below.

### Example: 225 lb for 8 reps

Your AMRAP set is 225 lb and you get 8 full reps before the bar stops moving. Run it through the two most used formulas:

- **Epley:** 225 × (1 + 8 ÷ 30) = **285 lb**
- **Brzycki:** 225 × 36 ÷ (37 − 8) = **279.31 lb**

Both are estimates of the single you could lift that day, not a weight you have lifted. Pick one formula and keep it, so the next AMRAP set compares with this one.

### One weight, any number of reps: 225 lb

An AMRAP set fixes the weight and lets the reps decide the estimate. Here is 225 lb at different rep counts:

| Reps at 225 lb | Epley | Brzycki |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 247.5 lb | 238.24 lb |
| 5 | 262.5 lb | 253.13 lb |
| 8 | 285 lb | 279.31 lb |
| 10 | 300 lb | 300 lb |
| 12 | 315 lb | 324 lb |

By Epley every extra rep at 225 lb adds 7.5 lb to the estimate: 7 reps give 277.5 lb and 8 reps give 285 lb. The two formulas meet at 10 reps. Below that Brzycki is the more cautious one, above it the more generous.

### The same in kilos: 100 kg for 8 reps

An AMRAP set of 100 kg for 8 reps estimates **126.67 kg** by Epley and **124.14 kg** by Brzycki. Had you stopped at 5 reps with the same bar, the estimates would be 116.67 kg and 112.5 kg. Estimate in the unit you lifted in; the formulas work the same in kg and lb.

### AMRAP sets in 5/3/1

In 5/3/1 the last set of weeks 1 to 3 is a plus set: 85% × 5+, 90% × 3+ and 95% × 1+ of the training max, with as many good reps as you can. A plus set is an AMRAP set, so the same formulas turn it into an estimated max, and lifters often compare that estimate from cycle to cycle to see whether they are getting stronger. The program's weights themselves still come from the training max, not from this estimate: see [the 5/3/1 training max](https://loadpr.com/guide/531-training-max/), or build a whole cycle with the [5/3/1 calculator](https://loadpr.com/531-calculator/).

### Getting an honest estimate from an AMRAP

- **Count only full reps you finished on your own.** A rep the spotter helped with is not a rep. At 225 lb, counting it as the 8th moves the Epley estimate from 277.5 lb to 285 lb.
- **Stop at the last good rep.** Reps with your form breaking down make a bigger number you cannot repeat next time.
- **Keep the set under about 12 reps.** At 225 lb for 15 reps, Epley gives 337.5 lb and Brzycki 368.18 lb. The longer the set, the more it tests endurance rather than strength.
- **Stay with one formula.** Switching formulas changes the number when your strength has not: 225 lb for 5 reps is 262.5 lb by Epley and 253.13 lb by Brzycki.

The guide [how 1RM is calculated](https://loadpr.com/guide/how-to-calculate-1rm/) compares the four formulas in the calculator, and the [rep max chart](https://loadpr.com/guide/rep-max-chart/) runs them backwards, from a max to the weight for each rep count.

### AMRAP sets in the LoadPR app

The LoadPR app estimates a 1RM from your logged sets with the Epley formula by default. With LoadPR+ you can pick another formula, such as Brzycki. Your current PR stays separate from the estimate: it is the heaviest weight you have logged, not a formula result. More in [PR tracking](https://loadpr.com/features/pr-tracking/).

### FAQ

**How do I estimate my 1RM from an AMRAP set?**
Multiply the weight by (1 + reps ÷ 30), the Epley formula. An AMRAP of 225 lb for 8 reps gives an estimated 1RM of 285 lb.

**What is my max if I can do 225 lb for 5 reps?**
About 262.5 lb by Epley and 253.13 lb by Brzycki.

**What is my 1RM if I lift 100 kg for 8 reps?**
About 126.67 kg by Epley and 124.14 kg by Brzycki.

**Does a rep with a spotter's help count in an AMRAP set?**
No. Count only reps you finished on your own. A spotted 8th rep at 225 lb would lift the Epley estimate from 277.5 lb to 285 lb.

**Is a 15-rep AMRAP set good for estimating a 1RM?**
It is less reliable than a shorter set. For 225 lb lifted 15 times, Epley gives 337.5 lb and Brzycki gives 368.18 lb.

# App features

## Plate loading on iPhone and Apple Watch

URL: https://loadpr.com/features/plate-loading/

Type a weight or pick a percentage, and LoadPR draws one side of the bar with the plates to put on it, each size in its own color. It works in pounds or kilograms, it is free to use as often as you like, and the same answer shows up on Apple Watch.

### What you see

The result screen has three parts. At the top is the weight you are loading, in large type, with the line that produced it underneath, such as 100% of 225 lbs. In the middle is one side of the barbell: the sleeve, the collar and then the plates, drawn bigger for heavier plates. Beside it is a short legend that counts each plate size, for example 2×45.

That is all you need to load the bar. Put the plates from the drawing on one sleeve, then the same plates on the other. The weight at the top already includes the bar, so 225 lb on a 45 lb bar means 90 lb of plates on each side: two 45 lb plates.

Under the drawing, LoadPR names the plate set it used, such as Standard (lbs), so you always know which bar and plates the answer assumes.

### How the plates are chosen

LoadPR takes the weight, removes the bar and splits what is left in two. Then it looks for plates that add up to exactly that amount per side. When more than one set of plates works, it picks the one with the most large plates, which is how most lifters load: big plates first, change plates last.

The search is exact, not a quick guess, and it respects how many plates of each size the set has, so it never draws a plate that is not there. For example, 180 lb on a 45 lb bar is 67.5 lb per side: one 45, two 10s and one 2.5.

Every plate size has its own color, in the drawing and in the legend, so you can match the picture to the rack at a glance. With the standard pound set:

### Pounds and kilograms

Pick lb or kg in Settings. In pounds, the free setup is a 45 lb bar with 45, 35, 25, 10, 5 and 2.5 lb plates. In kilograms, it is a 20 kg bar with 25, 20, 15, 10, 5, 2.5 and 1.25 kg plates.

For example, 100 kg on a 20 kg bar is 40 kg per side: one 25 and one 15.

The colors follow each plate's place in the set, not a competition color code. In kilograms the 25 is blue, the 20 teal, the 15 yellow, the 10 orange and the 5 red, and the small change plates are gray. The guide to Olympic plate colors below covers the colors used on competition plates.

### The free plate set

The free version loads from the standard set for your unit, with two of each plate per side. That covers most training: the heaviest exact load it can build is 535 lb with the pound set and 335 kg with the kilogram set.

Two of each per side changes some answers compared with a gym that has a stack of 45s. 315 lb is three 45s per side when plates are unlimited, but with two 45s per side LoadPR loads it as two 45s, one 35 and one 10. Both come to 135 lb per side.

If a target is heavier than the set can load, LoadPR shows the heaviest load the plates allow and adds a note with the real target, instead of quietly showing a smaller number.

With LoadPR+ you set up your own gyms: the bar, the plates and how many of each the gym has. Every answer then uses the plates that are really on the rack.

### When it helps

Between sets, when the next weight is a number on a program and you have a minute and a half to get it on the bar. In a gym you do not know, where the plates are not the ones you are used to. When you train in pounds and the program is written in kilograms, or the other way round.

### On Apple Watch and with Siri

The Apple Watch app shows the same plate drawing and legend for the lift and percentage you pick with the Digital Crown. It uses the plates your iPhone uses: the standard set in the free version, your own gym with LoadPR+.

You can also ask Siri: say “Calculate plates in LoadPR”, give the weight, and Siri reads out the plates for each side. The same action is in the Shortcuts app.

### Free to use

The plate calculator stays free. There is no daily limit and no count of how many weights you can load. The free version shows banner ads; LoadPR+ removes them and adds custom gyms, unlimited exercises and the other paid features.

### FAQ

**Does LoadPR show both sides of the bar?**
No. It draws one side, because both sides take the same plates. Load what you see on one sleeve, then repeat it on the other.

**Is the bar included in the weight LoadPR shows?**
Yes. The large number is the whole bar: the bar plus the plates on both sides. 225 lb on a 45 lb bar is two 45 lb plates per side.

**Why does LoadPR load 315 lb without three 45s per side?**
The free version has two of each plate per side, so it builds 315 lb from two 45s, one 35 and one 10 per side. That is the same 135 lb per side as three 45s.

**Can LoadPR use the plates my gym actually has?**
Yes, with LoadPR+. Set up a gym with its bar, its plates and how many of each it has, and every answer uses only those plates.

**What do the plate colors in LoadPR mean?**
They tell the sizes apart at a glance. In pounds the 45 is blue, the 35 teal, the 25 yellow, the 10 orange, the 5 red and the 2.5 gray. They are not the competition color code.

**Can I ask Siri which plates to load?**
Yes. Say “Calculate plates in LoadPR” and give the weight. Siri answers with the plates for each side, using the same plates as the app.

---

## Closest loadable weight

URL: https://loadpr.com/features/closest-loadable-weight/

Programs and percentages produce numbers like 187.5 lb that the plates on the rack can't make. LoadPR does not stop at an error: it shows the closest weight you can load and the plates for it, so you can get on with the set.

### Why some weights can't be loaded

A barbell is loaded in pairs. Every plate goes on both sleeves, so the total always goes up by twice the plate. With the standard pound set the smallest plate is 2.5 lb, which means the total moves in 5 lb steps: 185, 190, 195. A target of 187.5 lb sits between two of those steps.

In kilograms the standard set goes down to 1.25 kg plates, so the steps are 2.5 kg. A target of 102 kg falls between 100 kg and 102.5 kg.

Odd targets are common. Percentages rarely land on a step: 85% of 225 lb is 191.25 lb, and 90% is 202.5 lb.

### What LoadPR shows

LoadPR finds the heaviest load at or below your target and the lightest load at or above it, then shows whichever is closer. When both are the same distance away, it picks the lighter one.

For 187.5 lb on a 45 lb bar the two neighbors are 185 lb and 190 lb, each 2.5 lb away. LoadPR shows 185 lb: one 45 and one 25 per side. The line under the weight still says what you asked for, 100% of 187.5 lbs, so you know the bar is a little light.

For 191.25 lb the neighbors are 190 lb and 195 lb. 190 lb is closer, so LoadPR shows 190 lb: one 45, one 25 and one 2.5 per side.

The same rule runs on Apple Watch and in the Calculate Plates action for Siri, so all three give the same number.

### Down or up

Taking the nearer load means LoadPR sometimes goes a little over the target and sometimes a little under. For 202.5 lb, 200 lb and 205 lb are both 2.5 lb away, so the tie goes to the lighter 200 lb. For 203 lb, 205 lb is nearer, so LoadPR shows 205 lb: one 45 and one 35 per side.

If you would rather always stay under, or always go over, use the plate calculator on this website. It lists the closest load below and the closest load above, with the plates for each.

### When your plates are limited

The closest weight depends on the plates you have, not only on their sizes. The free version uses the standard set with two of each plate per side, and LoadPR searches that set exactly, so it never shows a load that needs a third 45.

With LoadPR+ you enter the plates your gym or garage really has, including how many of each. If a home gym has no small change plates, the steps get bigger, and LoadPR rounds to the loads those plates can make.

If a target is beyond what the plates can load at all, LoadPR shows the heaviest load they allow and adds a note with the real target, so you know the bar is short.

### How far off it can be

With the standard plates, the closest load is never more than half a step from the target: at most 2.5 lb with the pound set and 1.25 kg with the kilogram set. For training, that gap rarely matters, and you can always type a different number if your program needs an exact load.

### FAQ

**Why can't I load 187.5 lb on a barbell?**
With a 45 lb bar and plates down to 2.5 lb, the total moves in 5 lb steps, because every plate goes on both sides. 187.5 lb sits between 185 lb and 190 lb.

**Does LoadPR round up or down?**
To whichever loadable weight is closer. On a tie it takes the lighter one, so 187.5 lb becomes 185 lb and 191.25 lb becomes 190 lb.

**Will the closest weight ever need plates I don't have?**
No. LoadPR searches the plates in the set it is using, including how many of each, so every answer can be built from that set.

**Can I see both the load below and the load above?**
The app shows the closer one. The plate calculator on this website lists both, with the plates for each.

**What is the smallest step in kilograms?**
With 1.25 kg as the smallest plate, the total moves in 2.5 kg steps, such as 100 kg, 102.5 kg and 105 kg.

**Does Apple Watch show the same closest weight?**
Yes. The iPhone app, the Apple Watch app and the Calculate Plates action for Siri use the same rule and the same plates, so they agree.

---

## Percentages of your PR

URL: https://loadpr.com/features/percentages/

Most programs give the weight as a percentage. In LoadPR you turn a wheel to that percentage and get a weight you can load, with the plates for one side of the bar. The base is the current PR of the lift you pick, or any weight you type.

### The percentage wheel

Under the weight is a wheel of percentages from 50% to 120% in 5% steps. Swipe it or tap a value and the weight above changes at once, with the plates drawn below it.

The line under the weight says what you are looking at, such as 80% of 225 lbs. The large number is a weight you can load, and the drawing shows the plates for one side.

Values over 100% are there for overload work and for planning a new best. 105% of a 225 lb PR is 236.25 lb, and LoadPR shows 235 lb: two 45s and one 5 per side.

### What the percentage is of

When you pick a lift, the base is that lift's current PR: the heaviest weight you have logged for it, at any number of reps. If your best bench press entry is 225 lb for 3, the wheel works from 225 lb.

That is not an estimated one-rep max. LoadPR does not run your sets through a formula before taking the percentage; it uses the weight you actually lifted. If your program is written from a max you tested or estimated, type that number instead.

You can also skip the lift and type any weight. The wheel then works from that number, which is handy for a training max, a coach's number or a friend's lift.

### Rounded to a weight you can load

A percentage rarely lands on a weight the plates can make. LoadPR shows the closest weight you can load and the plates for it. On a 225 lb PR with the standard pound set:

There is no rounding setting to choose. The step comes from the plates: 5 lb with the standard pound set and 2.5 kg with the kilogram set. With LoadPR+ the steps follow your own gym's plates.

### Log a PR from the wheel

Next to the wheel is a plus button. Tap it after a set and LoadPR opens a new PR entry with the weight on screen already filled in. Add the reps (1 to 20), the date and a note if you want, and save.

If no lift is picked yet, LoadPR asks you to choose one first. When the new entry is your heaviest for that lift, it becomes the current PR, and every percentage on the wheel moves with it.

### On Apple Watch

The watch app has the same range. Pick a lift and turn the Digital Crown from 50% to 120% in 5% steps; it opens at 100%. The watch shows the weight to load and the plates for one side.

On the watch the base is the heaviest single you have logged for the lift, that is, your heaviest entry at 1 rep. A lift with no single logged yet does not appear on the watch.

The watch uses the same plates as your iPhone: the standard set in the free version, your own gym's plates with LoadPR+.

### Percentages on this website

The 1RM percentage calculator on this website works differently: it builds a full table from a one-rep max you enter, from 100% down to 50%, with a loadable weight for each row. Use it to plan a cycle on a laptop, and the wheel at the bar.

One small difference: when a percentage falls exactly halfway between two loads, the website's table rounds up and the app takes the lighter load. 90% of 225 lb is 205 lb in the table and 200 lb in the app.

### FAQ

**What is the LoadPR percentage wheel based on?**
On the selected lift's current PR, the heaviest weight you have logged for it at any number of reps. You can also type any weight and use that as the base.

**Are the percentages taken from an estimated max?**
No. LoadPR uses the heaviest weight you actually logged. If you want percentages of a tested or estimated max, type that number as the base.

**Why does 85% of 225 lb show 190 lb instead of 191.25?**
191.25 lb can't be built from the standard plates, so LoadPR shows the closest weight you can load: 190 lb, with one 45, one 25 and one 2.5 per side.

**Can I pick 82.5% or another value between the steps?**
Not on the wheel: it moves in 5% steps from 50% to 120%. For an in-between value, type the exact weight you want.

**Can I go above 100% on the wheel?**
Yes. The wheel goes up to 120%, which helps when you plan overload sets or a new PR attempt.

**Which lifts appear on the Apple Watch dial?**
Lifts with at least one logged single, that is, an entry at 1 rep. The watch uses the heaviest single as the base for its percentages.

---

## Gyms, bars and plates

URL: https://loadpr.com/features/gyms-and-plates/

Every answer in LoadPR is built from a plate setup: a bar, the plate sizes and how many of each you can put on the bar. The free version uses the standard set for pounds or kilograms. With LoadPR+ you save a setup for each gym you train in, so the calculator only uses plates that are really there.

### What a gym is in LoadPR

LoadPR calls a plate setup a gym. Each gym has a name, a unit (pounds or kilograms), a bar weight, the plate sizes and how many plates of each size there are. The calculator, the percentage wheel and the Apple Watch all load the bar from the gym that is selected, and its name appears under the plate drawing.

The count matters as much as the sizes. A plate set that can make any weight on paper is no help when the rack has one pair of 45s. LoadPR never draws a plate the gym does not have.

### The free setup

The free version comes with two gyms, Standard (lbs) and Standard (kg). Pick the one for your unit. Both have two of each plate per side:

That covers most training: the heaviest exact load is 535 lb with the pound set and 335 kg with the kilogram set. Two of each per side does change how some weights are built. 315 lb is two 45s, one 35 and one 10 per side instead of three 45s, which is the same 135 lb per side.

### Your own gyms with LoadPR+

With LoadPR+ you add a gym for each place you train: the commercial gym, the garage, the hotel gym on a work trip. For each one you set:

To switch, open Plate Setup and tap the gym. If the gym is in the other unit, the calculator switches to that unit as well, so a kilogram gym never gets pound plates.

### Plate counts: the plates you own

In the gym editor, each plate size has the total number of plates you own, both sides together, set in steps of two. Four 45s means two per side. A count of 0 means unlimited and shows as ∞, which suits a commercial gym with a full rack.

LoadPR uses those counts when it builds the bar. Take a garage gym with a 45 lb bar and one pair each of 45, 25, 10, 5 and 2.5 lb plates, and a program that asks for 245 lb. The most those plates can load is 220 lb, one of each per side. LoadPR shows 220 lb with a note that it is the heaviest load these plates allow, and the real target, so you know you are short instead of seeing a smaller number with no warning.

Below that limit, the counts still shape the answer. LoadPR looks for an exact load with the plates you have, and when there is none it shows the closest weight those plates can make.

### Bars and other plates

Not every bar weighs 45 lb or 20 kg. Set the bar weight for each gym and every total includes it. With a 35 lb bar and the standard plates, 95 lb is one 25 and one 5 per side. With a 15 kg bar, 60 kg is one 20 and one 2.5 per side.

Add Plate takes any plate weight in the gym's unit, so 15 lb plates or small change plates can be part of the setup. Each plate size has its own color in the drawing, and you can change it to match the plates in your gym.

### On Apple Watch

The watch uses the gym your iPhone has selected. In the free version that is the standard set for your unit; with LoadPR+ it is your own gym, with its bar, its plates and its counts. Change the gym on the iPhone and the watch gets the new plates from it.

### If LoadPR+ ends

Your gyms are kept. While LoadPR+ is not active, the calculator uses the standard set for the selected gym's unit. When LoadPR+ is active again, your gyms work as before.

### FAQ

**Which plates does the free version assume?**
The standard set for your unit, with two of each plate per side: a 45 lb bar with 45, 35, 25, 10, 5 and 2.5 lb plates, or a 20 kg bar with 25, 20, 15, 10, 5, 2.5 and 1.25 kg plates.

**How do I tell LoadPR how many plates I own?**
With LoadPR+, open the gym in Plate Setup and set the total for each plate size, both sides together. Four 45s means two per side, and 0 means unlimited.

**What happens when my plates can't make the weight?**
If the target is more than the plates can load, LoadPR shows the heaviest load they allow and a note with the real target. Below that, it shows the closest weight the plates can make.

**Can I use a bar that is not 45 lb or 20 kg?**
Yes, with LoadPR+. Set the bar weight for each gym, for example 35 lb or 15 kg, and every total includes it.

**Can I add plates the standard set does not have?**
Yes, with LoadPR+. Tap Add Plate in the gym editor and type the plate weight in the gym's unit.

**Can I change the color of a plate?**
Yes, with LoadPR+. Each plate size in a gym has a color, and you can change it to match your plates. The drawing and its legend use that color.

## PR tracking

URL: https://loadpr.com/features/pr-tracking/

LoadPR keeps a list of your lifts with the best weight for each one. Log a PR with its weight, reps, date and a note, and the app keeps the whole history. The current PR then feeds the percentage wheel, and your best singles go to the Apple Watch.

### Your lifts at a glance

The PR tab lists your exercises. Each row shows the name of the lift, its current PR and how long ago you set it, such as Bench Press, 225 lbs, 2 weeks ago. Tap a lift to see its PR history, newest first, with the number of entries.

Search the list by name, and sort it by name, by most recent or by heaviest PR.

### What a PR entry holds

Each entry has four parts:

Entries can be in different units. LoadPR compares them by their real weight, so a 100 kg single (220.46 lb) counts as heavier than a 220 lb single.

### What the current PR is

The current PR of a lift is the heaviest weight you have logged for it, at any number of reps. If your heaviest bench press entry is 225 lb for 3, the current PR is 225 lb. When two entries are equally heavy, the newer one counts.

That number is what the percentage wheel on the Load screen works from, so after a new best every percentage on the wheel moves up with it. The Apple Watch uses a stricter base: the heaviest single, an entry at 1 rep.

### Estimated one-rep max

A set of several reps also says something about your one-rep max. LoadPR estimates it with the Epley formula, written in the app as weight × (1 + 0.0333 × reps). 200 lb for 3 reps gives an estimated 1RM of 219.98 lb. A single is its own 1RM.

The estimate appears on the full progress chart, a LoadPR+ feature, as its own line next to the singles you actually lifted. With LoadPR+ you can also pick another formula in Settings. By the Brzycki formula, the same 200 lb triple comes to 211.76 lb.

### Three ways to log a PR

On the lift's page, tap + and fill in the entry. On the Load screen, tap the plus button next to the percentage wheel after a set, and the weight on screen is already filled in. Or ask Siri: say “Log a PR for Bench Press in LoadPR”, with the name of one of your lifts, and give the weight.

To fix a mistake, swipe the entry away in the history. Deleting an entry or a lift asks first, and it can be undone by shaking the iPhone.

### Free and LoadPR+

The free version tracks up to 5 exercises, and each one holds every PR you log. The list shows how many of the 5 you are using. LoadPR+ removes the exercise limit and adds the full progress chart, CSV export and import, iCloud sync through your own iCloud and the choice of formula.

### Widgets and Siri

The widgets show your records without opening the app: Top PR on the home screen or the lock screen, Recent PRs with your three latest records, and Progress Snapshot with your top lifts and their trend. Ask Siri “What's my Bench Press PR in LoadPR” and it answers with the weight and the date.

### FAQ

**What counts as the current PR in LoadPR?**
The heaviest weight you have logged for the lift, at any number of reps. When two entries weigh the same, the newer one counts.

**How does LoadPR estimate a one-rep max?**
With the Epley formula by default, written in the app as weight × (1 + 0.0333 × reps). 200 lb for 3 reps is an estimated 219.98 lb. With LoadPR+ you can pick another formula.

**How many reps can a PR entry have?**
From 1 to 20. A single, an entry at 1 rep, is also what the Apple Watch uses as the base for its dial.

**Can I log PRs in both kg and lb?**
Yes. Each entry keeps its own unit, and LoadPR compares entries by their real weight when it picks the current PR.

**How many exercises can I track for free?**
Five, and each one keeps every PR you log for it. LoadPR+ removes the exercise limit.

**Can I log a PR with Siri?**
Yes. Say “Log a PR for Bench Press in LoadPR”, with the name of one of your lifts, and give the weight. If you don't say the reps, LoadPR logs 1.

## Progress charts

URL: https://loadpr.com/features/progress-charts/

Each lift in LoadPR has a chart of its PRs over time. The blue line is what you actually lifted for a single; the gray line is the estimated one-rep max of your sets of more than one rep. Pick a range from 7 days to all time and touch the chart to read any entry.

### Two lines, one chart

The full chart draws two series. Actual PR is every entry logged at 1 rep, joined by a blue line. Est. 1RM is every entry with more reps, turned into an estimated one-rep max and joined by a lighter gray line. Keeping them apart shows the difference between a max you lifted and a max a formula predicts.

For example, a 225 lb single is plotted at 225 lb on the Actual PR line. A 205 lb set of 5 is plotted at 239.13 lb on the Est. 1RM line, by the app's Epley formula, weight × (1 + 0.0333 × reps). If you pick another formula in Settings, the gray line follows it.

### Ranges

Above the chart is a range picker: 7d, 30d, 90d, 1y and All. The chart opens on All. The header shows the best single in the range and the months the range covers, such as Nov 2024 – Aug 2026. If the range only has sets of several reps, the header shows the best estimate instead, marked Est.

If a lift has PRs but none in the range you picked, the chart says there are no entries in this range. Pick a wider range.

### Reading a point

Touch or drag across the chart and LoadPR picks the nearest entry, marks it with a line and shows its weight, with the month and year, in the header. Estimated points are labeled Est. Tap an empty part of the chart to clear the selection.

If a lift has entries in kg and in lb, the chart converts them to one unit, the unit of the lift's current PR, so every point shares one axis.

### The free mini chart

The free version has a mini chart on the Load screen. When you pick a lift, it shows your last 3 PRs at 1 rep, under the label PR Progress, with the latest weight on top.

Tap it to open the full chart. In the free version, that tap opens the LoadPR+ screen instead.

### Progress without opening the app

The Progress Snapshot widget, in the large size, shows your top lifts with their PR trend. On the lock screen, the rectangular Top PR widget shows a PR with its trend.

Ask Siri “Show my Bench Press progress in LoadPR” and it tells you how many PRs you have logged for the lift and your latest one.

### What the chart is for

A list of PRs tells you the best number. The chart tells you the direction: a line that climbs every month, a flat stretch that has lasted since spring, or an estimate from your sets of five that is running ahead of your last tested single. That last case is often the moment to test a new single.

### FAQ

**What is the gray line on the LoadPR chart?**
The estimated one-rep max of your entries with more than 1 rep. The blue line is your actual singles.

**Which formula does the chart use for the estimate?**
Epley by default. With LoadPR+ you can pick another formula in Settings, and the chart follows it.

**Why does my chart say there are no entries?**
The lift has PRs, but none in the range you picked. Switch to a wider range such as 1y or All.

**Is the progress chart free?**
The mini chart of your last 3 singles is free, on the Load screen. The full chart with its ranges and the estimated 1RM line is part of LoadPR+.

**Can I chart a lift logged in both kg and lb?**
Yes. The chart converts every entry to the unit of the lift's current PR, so all points share one axis.

## Workout timer

URL: https://loadpr.com/features/workout-timer/

The Timer tab has four modes. Rest counts down the break between sets and is free. EMOM, HIIT and AMRAP are interval timers for conditioning work and come with LoadPR+. Each mode remembers the timers you run, so the next one is a tap away.

### Rest timer, free

Set the rest with two wheels, minutes from 0 to 59 and seconds in steps of 15, and tap Start. The shortest rest is 15 seconds. Until you have recents, LoadPR suggests 30 s, 1 min, 1:30, 2 min, 3 min and 5 min, and a tap on one starts it.

While it runs, the countdown shows on the lock screen and in the Dynamic Island as a Live Activity, and if you allow notifications, one tells you when the time is up. You can lock the phone between sets and still see the time left.

### EMOM, with LoadPR+

Every minute on the minute: pick 1 to 60 rounds of one minute each and the timer runs them back to back. The screen shows the seconds left in the minute and the round, such as Round 1 of 10, and the iPhone taps at the start of each new round.

The suggestions are 5, 8, 10, 12, 15 and 20 rounds.

### HIIT, with LoadPR+

Set the work time and the rest time, each from 5 to 120 seconds in steps of 5, and 1 to 20 rounds. LoadPR shows the total time before you start. While it runs, WORK and REST alternate in green and red, with the round below the countdown.

The suggestions cover common intervals:

### AMRAP, with LoadPR+

As many rounds as possible: set a time from 1 to 60 minutes and start. Tap Round Complete at the end of each round. The screen counts your rounds and shows the time of the last one.

When the time is up, LoadPR shows the rounds completed, your average pace, the fastest and the slowest round, and the split of every round. Like Rest, AMRAP shows on the lock screen and in the Dynamic Island while it runs, with your round count.

### Recents and pins

Each timer you start is saved in that mode's recents, up to 10, so you can run it again with one tap. Pin the ones you use most: pinned timers stay at the top and are never pushed off the list. Swipe a recent to remove it.

### At the gym

The screen stays on while a timer runs. You can switch to the Load or PR tab, for example to load the next set or log the last one, and the timer keeps going. When a timer finishes, the iPhone plays a sound.

EMOM and HIIT do not have a Live Activity, so keep LoadPR open to follow their rounds. Rest and AMRAP show on the lock screen.

### FAQ

**Which timer modes are free?**
Rest is free. EMOM, HIIT and AMRAP are part of LoadPR+.

**Does the rest timer work with the phone locked?**
Yes. The Rest countdown shows on the lock screen and in the Dynamic Island, and if you allow notifications, one tells you when the rest is over.

**What is the shortest and longest rest I can set?**
From 15 seconds to 59 minutes 45 seconds, in steps of 15 seconds.

**What does the Tabata suggestion set?**
The HIIT timer with 20 seconds of work and 10 seconds of rest for 8 rounds, 4 minutes in all. HIIT is part of LoadPR+.

**Does the AMRAP timer count my rounds?**
Yes. Tap Round Complete after each round. At the end LoadPR shows the rounds, your average pace, the fastest and slowest round and every split.

**Does the timer keep running if I switch tabs?**
Yes. It keeps running while you use the Load or PR tab, and the screen stays on while it runs.

---

## LoadPR on Apple Watch

URL: https://loadpr.com/features/apple-watch/

The LoadPR watch app puts the percentage dial on your wrist. Pick a lift, turn the Digital Crown to the percentage your program asks for, and read the weight to load. Tap the weight for the plates on one side of the bar. It is part of the free version.

### Your lifts

The watch lists your lifts from A to Z, each with its best single: the heaviest entry you have logged at 1 rep. A lift with no single yet does not appear; log a 1-rep PR on the iPhone and it shows up.

The lifts and the plates come from the iPhone app. The watch keeps the last ones it received, so it does not need the iPhone in your hand at the rack.

### The dial

Tap a lift and the dial opens at 100% of its best single. Turn the Digital Crown and the percentage moves in 5% steps, from 50% to 120%, with a click on your wrist at each step. The large number is the weight to load, and the line below it says what it is, such as 100% of 225.

Above 100% the ring and the label turn red, and the watch gives a warning tap as you cross 100%, so an overload set is never a surprise.

### Plates on your wrist

Tap the weight to open Plates. It draws one side of the bar with the plates in their colors, the weight, and a count of each plate, such as 1×45, 1×35 and 1×5. When the weight is the bar alone, it says Just the bar.

For example, 95% of a 225 lb single is 213.75 lb. The plates can't make that, so the watch shows 215 lb, the closest load: one 45, one 35 and one 5 per side.

### The same answer as the iPhone

The watch rounds the same way as the iPhone, to the closest weight the plates can make, so both show the same working weight for the same base and percentage. It uses the gym your iPhone has selected: the standard plates in the free version, two of each per side, or your own gym with LoadPR+.

One difference is the base. The iPhone's percentage wheel works from the lift's current PR at any reps; the watch works from the best single. If your heaviest bench press entry is 225 lb for 3 and your best single is 215 lb, the iPhone works from 225 lb and the watch from 215 lb.

### Requirements

The watch app needs an Apple Watch with watchOS 11 or later, paired with an iPhone that runs LoadPR on iOS 26 or later. There is nothing extra to buy for it.

### When it helps

At the rack, with the phone in a bag or across the room. During percentage work, where the weight changes every set. With chalk on your hands, when a turn of the crown is easier than typing a number.

### FAQ

**Do I need an Apple Watch to use LoadPR?**
No. Everything works on the iPhone. The watch app adds the percentage dial and the plates on your wrist.

**Which watchOS does LoadPR need?**
watchOS 11 or later, on an Apple Watch paired with an iPhone running iOS 26 or later.

**Can I log a PR on the watch?**
No. The watch shows your lifts, the dial and the plates. Log PRs on the iPhone, or ask Siri on the iPhone.

**Does the watch need my iPhone nearby?**
Not for what it already has: it keeps the last lifts and plates it received. New PRs and a new gym reach it from the iPhone app.

**Why does the watch dial turn red?**
The percentage is above 100% of your best single. The watch also gives a warning tap as you cross 100%.

**Does the watch use the same plates as my iPhone?**
Yes. It uses the gym selected on the iPhone: the standard set in the free version, your own gym with LoadPR+.
